From the books of [Iorinis Georgij?] of Werdeß, counselor of review to the most serene Elector of Bavaria.

Six Books of Polygraphy

By Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim

Addressed to Emperor Maximilian

There has been added one book, the Key to Polygraphy, by the same author.

Contained in these books is the method by which one person can communicate to another whatever he wishes, not only secretly, but sometimes even without suspicion. They also present a method most useful both in teaching and in learning. Furthermore, they provide the capacity for understanding the deepest mysteries of the arts and disciplines.

There have also been added explanations of certain passages, especially of those in which the principles of the admirable work Steganography lie hidden; these indeed offer to the ingenious an occasion for discovering things far greater and subtler. By the very learned man Adolph von Glauburg, patrician of Frankfurt.

Frankfurt, 1550

Dedication to Emperor Maximilian

The letter of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James of Würzburg, on the Polygraphia

I was hesitating, wavering in mind, most invincible Maximilian Caesar, and doubting somewhat within myself whether or not I should be doing something worthwhile, were I to dedicate the volume of our Polygraphy to your Caesarean majesty. For among the great [you are] the greatest, among the more powerful the most powerful, among all the wise by far the wisest—to whom, therefore, nothing ought to be inscribed except what is great, nothing dedicated except what is elaborated with the highest erudition. But I, having attained little or nothing of literary erudition, not without reason hesitated the longer whether I ought to bring my trifles before so great a majesty: since I am neither suited in talent to elaborate anything, nor adorned with the necessary charm of speech. For I know, and cannot deny, how scanty is my furniture, how rude my talent, and that I have no vein of eloquence in speaking—on account of which, with just consideration, I held back for some time, and dreaded, an inept writer, to appear before your glorious majesty. For since after God you are by right lord of the world,

it is no wonder if I, unlearned and the least of monks, should fear the censure of so great a majesty as yours, and dread to offer those lucubrations of mine which I know to be unworthy of your hands. And while I was revolving these things in my mind, there came a messenger with letters sent from your highness, by which you summoned me to Cologne, the expenses necessary for the journey having already some time before been appointed through another. But when I had read over the letters of your serenity, confidence soon conquered my bashfulness, and the consideration of your innate gentleness put my fear to flight. For I know your nature to be most mild—you who, since you are the most modest of all, are wont both to grow gentle toward the humble and to resist the proud. You know not how to be vainly exalted, nor, in the manner of tyrants, to despise the humble who are devoted to your highness; for just as you have nothing by which to grow on earth, so no envy will penetrate your mind. You are the greatest; many and great things, too, you have accomplished no less bravely than wisely, both in peace and in war, by which you have both won an eternal name and are celebrated with the reverence of the highest honor, the affection and favor of all your subjects. These are the riches of princes: the love and favor of the people, and to do justice to each according to the precept of the charity of God. Since, therefore, all bear your name to the stars with praises, and all proclaim you most mild and most humane, why should I, singularly, suspect you to be more severe [toward me]? Thereafter [there is] no

it was not, especially when by your letter you deign to entice me to write. Thus, at last encouraged by weighing these things, I laid aside all fear and took up great confidence in your innate gentleness. Indeed, since all draw confidence from the fountain of your piety, why should I alone not approach trustfully? You, who are always gracious, gentle, and pious to all, surely cannot be cruel to me alone. Therefore, with that humility which is fitting, and which I owe and am able to show, I approach the throne of your most excellent majesty, prostrate upon the ground: I devotedly offer the aforementioned work of Polygraphy, and humbly commend my littleness to your serenity as a servant to his lord. Therefore now accept, most gracious Caesar, the very small little gift which I bring, in which may you deign to weigh my spirit, most subject to you, not its value. But in the subject system of the Polygraphy there are, in certain places, some mysteries wrapped in riddles, lest the meaning of the more inward art which lies hidden should become manifest to the understanding of all. Just as not all things befit all people, so not all things everywhere and always suit everyone. There are therefore certain mysteries shut up here, which in my judgment can be more useful and more necessary to none than to princely men. For the more people they are concerned with, the greater caution of secrecy must be applied to their counsels. For this book teaches princes to command secrecy for their secrets.

But because your Caesarean majesty, occupied with many affairs, does not have time to search out those things which lie hidden wrapped in mysteries, lest he be deprived of the fruit of my labor, I have appended a little explanatory book of the whole work, which I have entitled the Key of Polygraphy; with it as guide you will more easily understand everything obstructed here by figures. May God preserve you unharmed for our salvation. I wrote on the twenty-sixth day of the month of April, in the year of Christ 1508.

Table or Index of the Lucubrations of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot first of Sponheim and afterward of St. James at Würzburg.

Johannes Trithemius the abbot was born in the village of Trittenheim, in the diocese of Trier, on the banks of the river Moselle, on the first day of the month of February, at the eleventh hour, in the thirtieth minute after midday, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1462, in the tenth indiction of the Romans: his father was Johannes de Heidenberg, and his mother was called Elisabeth de Longo Vico. This was in that year, namely, in which the city of Mainz, in the dissension of two pontiffs, was captured, lost its liberty, and found servitude, with many of its citizens driven into exile; in the fourth current year of Pope Pius, the second of that name, and the twenty-second of Emperor Frederick III. But in the year of the Lord 1482, in the monastery of Sponheim in the diocese of Mainz, on the first day of February, that is, the day on which he had once been born, he laid aside the secular habit, and there assumed the monastic habit under the rule of the divine father Benedict, according to the observance newly introduced. In the following year, which was the eighty-third above the four-hundredth and the thousandth, after Johannes de Colenhusen the abbot had been transferred to Seligenstadt by canonical postulation, Johannes Trithemius, by the common election of the brethren, was promoted and ordained abbot of the aforementioned monastery of Sponheim on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, and presided for twenty-three years, one month, and nineteen days. When these had passed, not without many labors, provoked by the rashness of certain rivals, he accepted the abbacy of St. James at Würzburg, which was offered to him, and of his own free will resigned Sponheim, full of useless cares. In both places he wrote several little works, from which, recently on a sheet in his own hand, to me

he recorded the following. Since you, as a friend, ask me for their titles, I gladly assent to your wishes, so that from the consideration of such great labors of his you may have a more exact memory of our common friend and teacher. And first I shall record the titles of those lucubrations which he laboriously composed while he was abbot at Sponheim. First he wrote the constitutions of his order, which were made in the provincial chapters by command of the presidents, one book. On the visitation of monks, one book. On the manner of celebrating a provincial chapter, one book. On the Rule of Saint Benedict, two books. Homilies and exhortatory sermons to his monks, two books, which he dedicated to his predecessor. On the temptations of cloistered persons and their remedies, two books. To Nicholas, priest of Mernic, on the priestly life, one book. Against the private property of monks, one book. A penthic work, that is, a mournful one, on the ruin of his order, one book. On the illustrious men of his order, four books. Praises of the order of the Carmelite brothers, two books. To Gerlach, abbot of Deutz, praises of manual writers, one book. To Johann Dalberg, bishop of Worms, on ecclesiastical writers, one book. On the praises of Saint Anne, grandmother of the Lord, one book. Chronicle or annals of the monastery of Hirsau, two large volumes. Chronicle of the succession of the dukes of Bavaria and the counts palatine, to Philip, count palatine and elector, one book. Life of Saint Irmina, nun and first abbess at [Horrio?] in Trier, one book. On the misery of cloistered prelates, two books. Praises of Saint Andrew the Apostle, one book. Praises of the monastic life, one book. Praises of true penitence, one book. Monocollogion of a man devoted to God, addressed to himself, one book. On the miracles of the holy mother Anne, one book. To Ulrich, canon of Cologne, on questions concerning the Gospel of John, one book. To the same, on questions concerning the Psalms, one book. To the presidents of the annual chapter concerning the Bursfelde observance, he abridged the statutes of the same union, one book. An epitome or breviary of the same, one book. On ecclesiastical computus, one book. The spiritual exercise of monks, one book. To Jacob Wimpfeling of [unclear], one book. On the illustrious writers of Germany, to Jacob [unclear]. Letters from Sponheim to various persons, four books. Orations delivered in chapters and elsewhere are twenty-four in number, which make one book. He wrote forty very fine sermons to his brothers of the monastery of Sponheim, one book. Sermons on feast days to the people, one book. Several supplicatory prayers to God and the saints, one book. From Greek speech he translated into Latin Maximus the abbot on the incarnation of the Lord. Also the anathema of Saint Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria, against the heretics, promulgated in the third synod of Ephesus; and certain letters of the same synod. He also wrote for the edification of monks a notable work which he entitled On the Threefold Region of Cloistered Persons, three books. He also wrote certain other smaller works, whose titles he did not record for me. These, most loving brother Nicholas, are the Trithemian works which, during the twenty-three years in which he was abbot at Sponheim, he wrote by lamplight for the honor of God, amid cares and continual occupation with household affairs, reading or writing day and night whenever he was able to steal leisure for himself. During the years in which he presided he brought into the library of Sponheim a very great treasure of books in every discipline, not only by the art of printing but also by the hand of scribes. For when I was with him for the space of one year, to learn Greek and Hebrew letters from him, I counted two thousand volumes in the library, of which at least eight hundred had been properly written by pen on parchment and paper. I often heard from his own mouth that he had spent more than two thousand florins on books, which he had not received from the substance of the monastery, which was always very slender, but

Ad eundem eiufdem Polygraphiae clauem, librum unum. Responsiones ad octo quaestiones eiusdem Caesaris, librum unum. Ad eundem de septem intelligentijs mouentibus orbes, librum unum. Ad Ioachim Marchionem Brandenburgensem principem electorem, uariarum quaestionum, orationum, &; propositionum libros duos. Ad eundem de praenotationibus licitis Christiano, et non licitis, libros duos. Ad eundem scripsit mirandum &; laboriosum opus illud Steganographiae libros octo, quod temerarius ille Bouillus nōcapiens imperitissime &; falsißime repraehendit. Ad eundem principesmę epistolarū, librum unum. Ad euandem contra maleficos, &; omnes artes, &; superstitiones ab ecclesia prohibitas, libros quinqƺ. Ad eundem de causis &; cura morbi caduci, ac maleficorum, libros tres. Ad Iacobum Trithemium fratrem suum itinerarium uitae suae, libros duos. Ad Burghardum de Hornec medicum de peculio monialiũ, librum unum. Historiam siue annales de origine, regibus, &; gestis populi Francorum &; Germanorum scripsit tria magna uolumina, narrationem incipiens à Marcomero rege, qui populum anno ante incarnationem domini quadringentesimo tricesimo tertio, à Scythiae finibus in Germaniam eduxit ad ostiuꝰ Ostia Rheni, usque inuice sinum oclauum et nomū annulum Maximiliani Caesaris. Ad Laurentium Wirciburgensem episcopum, orientalisque Fran- ciae ducem, epithoma siue breuiariū scripsit corundem triū uoluminium historiarū, libros tres. Ad eundē de ducibus et episcopis Francorum Wir- ciburgensiū, librum unum. De miraculis ad memoriam dominae nostrae sanctae Mariae apud Dittelbach ostensis libros duos. De miraculis eiufdem in urticeto apud Helprunnam ostensis, libros sex. Apologeticum in Caro- lum Bouillum, ea quae non intellexit calumniantem, librum unum. De ori- gine et regibus Francorum, librum unum. Chronicon monasterij sui, cui nunc praesidet, diui Iacobi apud Wircburg, librum unum. Ad Alber- tum ex marchionibus Brandenburgij, archiepiscopum Moguntinum et Magdeburgẽsem, uitam diuini Rabani archipraesulis, libros tres. De cius- dem a Magunciaco translatione in Saxoniam, librum unum. Ad eundem uitā sancti Maximi episcopi, librum unum. Ad Ioannē comitē palatinum, Bauariaeq́; ducem et comitem in Spanheim, apud Symeren residentem, de origine, regibus, ac ducibus Bauarorum simul et comitum palatinorum et Spanheimensium, libros quatuor. De demonibus et artibꝰ profanis, ma- leficis et superstitiosis laboriosum opus uersat in manibus, quod libris ha- bebit duodecim, inquibus omnia diabolicarum artium uaframenta explo- dit, confundit et euertit. Epistolarum Herbipolensium, quas in cascripsit abbatia, libros quatuor. Scripsit etiam alia minora complura, suae et amicorum deuotioni congrua, ut sunt. Cursus, rosarium, missale officium, & uarie orationes, simul et prosae sequentiae de sancta Anna saluato- ris nostriauiā. Scripsit et de sancto Maria Magdalena laudes, precationes atque rosarium De sancto Ioseph nutritio domini rosarium. De sancto Pe- tro apostolo rosarium. De sancclo Ioanne euangelista rosarium. Ad imstan- tiā Ioannis archiepiscopi Treuirorum sequentiam de Anna, quae incipit. Iesu coelorū regis, sub melodia, Aue praeclarae. Aliā in eius festo canēdam: quae incipit Exultent in hac die. Tertiā ad provincialē carmelitarū Augu- stae, et incipit Iubilemus in honore. Quartā de sancta Hildegarde virgine quae sic incipit Laus fit tibi dominae rex aeternae gloriae. Quintā de sancto ** iij

and since he was dear to princes, the gifts with which he was honored by them he spent, for the most part, on books. For he is the greatest lover and cultivator of books, beyond all whom I know today living in the flesh. It is said by many, however, that his successor, who is now abbot in Sponheim, has alienated many volumes; whether this is true, I certainly do not at all know. In the year of the Lord 1504, when a fierce war had arisen between the kingdom and Philip, count palatine, Trithemius, from fear of the enemy, withdrew with his library and the possessions of the monastery to Kreuznach, a nearby town, and I likewise returned to my own affairs. But in the year 1506, in the month of October, Trithemius himself, spurred on by the envy of certain men, accepted the abbacy of Saint James at Würzburg, and resigned that of Sponheim. There, in quiet, he writes various works, whose titles and number he sent to me through these persons when asked.

To Emperor Maximilian he published a wonderful work, which he entitled Polygraphia, six books. To the same man, a key to the same Polygraphia, one book. Responses to eight questions of the same emperor, one book. To the same man, on the seven intelligences that move the spheres, one book. To Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg and prince elector, two books of various questions, orations, and propositions. To the same man, two books on foreknowledges lawful and not lawful for a Christian. To the same man he wrote that wonderful and laborious work of Steganographia, eight books, which that rash Bouillus, not understanding it, criticized most ignorantly and most falsely. To the same prince, one book of letters. To the same man, against sorcerers and all arts and superstitions prohibited by the Church, five books. To the same man, on the causes and cure of epilepsy and of sorcerers, three books. To Jacob Trithemius his brother, an itinerary of his life, two books. To Burkhard von Horneck, physician, on the private property of nuns, one book. He wrote a history or annals on the origin, kings, and deeds of the people of the Franks and Germans, three large volumes, beginning the narrative from King Marcomer, who in the year 433 before the incarnation of the Lord led the people from the borders of Scythia into Germany to the mouths of the Rhine, down to the twenty-eighth and ninth year of Emperor Maximilian.

To Lorenz, bishop of Würzburg and duke of East Francia, he wrote an epitome or breviary of the same three volumes of histories, three books. To the same man, on the dukes and bishops of the Franks of Würzburg, one book. On the miracles shown at the memorial of Our Lady Saint Mary at Dettelbach, two books. On the miracles of the same woman shown in the nettle-patch at Heilbronn, six books. An apologetic work against Charles Bouillus, who calumniated things he did not understand, one book. On the origin and kings of the Franks, one book. A chronicle of his monastery, over which he now presides, Saint James at Würzburg, one book. To Albert, of the margraves of Brandenburg, archbishop of Mainz and Magdeburg, the life of the divine Rabanus, archprelate, three books. On his translation from Mainz into Saxony, one book. To the same man, the life of Saint Maximus, bishop, one book. To Johann, count palatine, duke of Bavaria and count in Sponheim, residing at Simmern, on the origin, kings, and dukes of the Bavarians, together with the counts palatine and those of Sponheim, four books. He has in hand a laborious work on demons and profane, magical, and superstitious arts, which will have twelve books, in which he demolishes, confounds, and overturns all the deceits of the diabolical arts. Of the Würzburg letters, which he wrote in that abbacy, four books.

He also wrote several other smaller works, suited to his own devotion and that of his friends, such as: courses, a rosary, a missal office, and various prayers, together with prose sequences on Saint Anne, the grandmother of our Savior. He also wrote praises, prayers, and a rosary on Saint Mary Magdalene. A rosary on Saint Joseph, foster-father of the Lord. A rosary on Saint Peter the apostle. A rosary on Saint John the evangelist. At the instance of Johann, archbishop of Trier, a sequence on Anne, which begins: Jesu, king of the heavens, to the melody Ave praeclara. Another to be sung on her feast, which begins: Let them rejoice on this day. A third to the provincial of the Carmelites at Augsburg, and it begins: Let us jubilate in honor. A fourth on Saint Hildegard the virgin, which begins thus: Praise is made to you, Lord, king of eternal glory. A fifth on Saint

Multas quoque deuotißimas meditaciones et amp; orationes de domino nostro Iesu Christo, de sanctissima eius genitrice uirgine Maria, atque de uarijs sanctis pulchra uarietate composuit: cum ingentibus alijs, quae uidebit et amp; mirabitur deuota posteritas omnis. Haec sunt mi Nicolae charißime Trithemij abbatis nostri uolumina, quae per annos ferè triginta continuo lucubrauit studio: praeter illa quae nondum perfecta in manibus uersantur sub incude mihi incognita. Vale, ex aedibus meis Duraclusanis: quinta mensis Octobris, Anno salutis nostrae millefimo quingentesimo quinto decimo, Ioannes Duraclusius. LEgimus complures ueterum sapientes, philosophos, reges et amp; prin¬ cipes, olim uarios atq́; multiplices excogitauisse modos, quibus nun cijs suis ad loca remotiora mittendis tuto committerent arcana con silij, &amp; quicquid mysterij confidendum occurrisset secreti, quo fierent in perferendis idonei, atq́; ab omni prauorum incursione securi, ne uel sim¬ plicitas cabalisticorum denudaret mysterium, uel bacutiorum innata cu¬ riositas apostolicis rebus infermentum. Magnus ex his Romano¬ rum Caesar Augustus, tenebroso cupiens in arduis uti nunciorum ministe¬ rio, spiramina uocis conceptae mutauit ex lucidis in opaca, quorum barba¬ riem uotis renitentem, meta theseos orchemate pulchra inuentione ad nu tum conuenientem effecit. Et iste receptiuus et amp; quasi perpetuus ordo the Iemati nihilominus et amp; temporis rationi subiectus, quanquam nuncios ab in cursione bacuceorum conseruet in uia securos: sui tamen regulatas non custodiens metas, intuentes faciet omnes de suspicione rei sollicitos. Archimedes ille Syracusius mathematicorum facilè princeps, albam suis conuenientem institutis uolucrem, nudam per caput et amp; pedes, bactro in formam tetragoni reciso, circumferenter affixit, ordinatisq́; debita pro¬ portione ministris, opus uolatili commendauit instrumento, donec in pic cam imago uolucris albe mutata comparuit. Quo ritè peracto, resoluit affixam sua manu, quam ut auolare permisisset, facta est subito inter fami liares penetralium facies disiunctio magna, surrexitq́; mox tortuosae ima[unclear]** iij

...for Rupert, duke of the Bingii, which begins, “Let them exult on this day.” The sixth, on Saint Joseph, foster-father of the Lord; and it begins thus, “Let us sing, illustrious ones.”

The seventh, on Saint Rabanus, archbishop. The eighth, on the wounds of Christ, which begins thus, “Let us adore Jesus Christ, let us lament with him crucified.” The ninth, on the compassion of blessed Mary ever virgin; and it begins thus, “Come, let us weep with devout mind, sharing the suffering of the blessed virgin Mary”: that is, to the melody “Ave praeclara.” The tenth, on Saint Joachim, father of Our Lady, which begins thus, “Let us adore the Trinity, let us praise together the unity, of Father, Son, and Spirit.” The eleventh, on the good proper angel of each person. The twelfth, for the proper Mass of each priest. The thirteenth, on Saint Maximus, bishop of Mainz. The fourteenth, on Saint Mary the Virgin, Christ’s hostess. The fifteenth, on Saint Mary Magdalene.

The sixteenth, on Saint Mary of Egypt. The seventeenth, on Saint James the Greater, apostle. The eighteenth, on Saint Andrew, apostle. The nineteenth, on Saint Benedict, abbot. The twentieth, on All Saints. And for each of the named [unclear] saints he composed individual new offices of the Mass, conformable to the divine Scriptures. He wrote besides a little work of meditations and prayers on the Lord’s incarnation, nativity, life, passion, and death, suited to devotion, in two books. The Mirror of Heavenly Doctrine, of no small service to compunction of mind, one book, which begins thus, “The beginning of human salvation.” He also composed many most devout meditations and prayers on our Lord Jesus Christ, on his most holy mother the Virgin Mary, and on various saints, with beautiful variety, together with very many other things, which all devout posterity will see and admire. These, my dearest Nicolaus, are the volumes of Trithemius our abbot, which through almost thirty years he has worked out with continual study by lamplight, besides those which, not yet completed, are in his hands under the anvil and unknown to me. Farewell, from my house at Duraclusa, on the fifth of the month of October, in the year of our salvation 1515. Johannes Duraclusius.

From the letter of Johannes Duraclusius, his disciple, to Nicolaus Hamerius Emelanus.

Preface of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James at Würzburg, to Emperor Maximilian, on Polygraphy.

We have read that many wise men of the ancients, philosophers, kings, and princes, once devised varied and manifold methods by which they might safely entrust to their messengers, when sending them to more remote places, the secrets of counsel and whatever secret mystery had to be confided, so that they would become fit for carrying them and secure from every assault of the wicked, lest either the simplicity of the cabalists should lay bare the mystery, or the innate curiosity of the [bacutii?] should bring leaven into apostolic matters. Great among these, Augustus, Caesar of the Romans, wishing in difficult affairs to use the service of messengers in obscurity, changed the breathings of the conceived voice from clear signs into obscure ones; and, by a beautiful invention, through the measure of transposition, he made their barbarous form, resistant to wishes, agree with his command in a dance-like arrangement. And this receptive and, as it were, perpetual order, nevertheless subject to the theme and to the reckoning of time, although it keeps the messengers safe on the road from the assault of the [bacucei?], yet, by not keeping the regulated bounds of its own system, will make all who look on anxious with suspicion of the matter.

Archimedes of Syracuse, easily the foremost of mathematicians, took a white bird suited to his own arrangements, bare at head and feet, fixed it around a staff cut into the form of a tetragon, and, after arranging the attendants in due proportion, entrusted the work to a flying instrument, until the image of the white bird appeared changed into a magpie. When this had been duly done, he released with his own hand what had been fixed; and when he had allowed it to fly away, there was suddenly among the familiar faces of the inner chambers a great separation, and soon there arose [unclear].

ꝑmis monasticae prius monstrum nimis uagabundum, cuiusin aspectu ne- mo quod erat, potuit cogitare. Nec prius conquieuit bubonum dissensio, donec imago magistri, picam scitè religasset tetragano confimili. Marcus T. Cicero facundus orator, ingenio usus &; arte, phraseos minu- tias commutauit in signa, &; thelematos sui philergiam siue characterem pro usitata phrasi locauit. Tāta uero in hac ipsa nouitate usus est copia, ut rebus pene cunctis in mundo, eius sufficere poßit inventio. His autem mysteriorum praenunciatoribus artis institutio mirandam contulit agilita tem, ut praeter naturam omnium solidis integris bonae magistri subser- uiant voluntati. Quorum rex tutißime uti semper potest obsequio, quam uis non sine magno labore, manifestaq́; bucaceorum suspitione. Cyprianus vero Carthaginensis ecclesiae sanctissimus praesul &; martyr, ipsa Cicero nianae institutionis documenta, Christianorum uolens prouidere utilitati, baud mediocriter ampliauit, &; quae nostris defuerant moribus, adiunxit. Pharamundus quoque tertius &; quadragesimus post Marcomerum Fran- corum in Germania rex potentißimꝰ, cum anno dominicae natiuitatis qua dringentesimo uicesimo quarto, fines Gallorum potenter intraret, ut fie- rent omnia tuto, suis arcanis alligauit minutias peregrinas. Clodius etiam Crinitus maior natu filius, patri succedens in regno Francorum, poste aquam totam Galliam suo uiolenter subiugas- et imperio, Gallos omnes ut uictos &; servos depilari, &; barba radi prae- cepit, Francos autem Gallorum uictores &; dominos, comam nutrire man- dauit, &; barbam. Vnde &; crinitus est dictus. Imitatione genitoris my- steria consilij notis iniuoluit proprijs ac peregrinis. Carolus magnus cognomine, tertius &; sexagesimus post Marcomerum Francorum rex, qui primus ex Francis im̄erauit Romanis, Nannone grammatico praeceptore, linguam Germanicam, quae illi fuit paterna, in- star latinae cupiens exornare Grammaticis, arduum opus incepit, quod tamen multis implicitus, &; morte praeuentus non perfecit. Bubones minutijs alligauit &; uarijs, &; multis, quo maiorem Brabantia natum. Siue Namurci Germania non habuit. Singulis regni praefectis, singulosos contulit arte bubones. Nortmanni ex Gothiae finibus egreßi, cum olim crudeliter Galliam deuastarent, uocatis è Groecia bubonibus, tutum suis latibulum parauerunt arcanis, quod hodie paucis est notum. Beda noster in Anglia monachus, Nortmannorum facti non ignarus, plura his similia ueterum descripsit inuenta, quibus iter mysterijs lucidum fecerunt opacum. Ipse artrologiam primus memoriae posteritatis commendauit, &; dactilogiam inuenit. Fuerunt qui accidentijs uisibilibus minuta discernerent, quorum prudentia nox uertebatur in diem, et sine bubonum ministerio lux splendebat in tenebris. De his autem Steganographiae nostrae quondã sollicitator illustris comes palatinus princeps elector, documenti à nobis manifestum suscepit experimentum. Alij uero minutias diuisione regulata multiplicantes, barbarorum ad instar, naturae schemata subuerterunt, in tenebris orchemata nascentium umbra secretantes, &; ubi consilij requirebat arcanum, perdiapyrana ta cabalam subministrabant absentibus. Magnus in his labor est annosaq́; mentis exercitatio longa, in qua nemmo fit repente peritus ad usum. Omnia necessitas suffert. Fuerunt etiam quos harmonia coelestis peregrinas docuit componere uoces, quarunduplex fuit intelligentibus usus, dum alter sensum suspendebat, alter incetheramentem. Deus omnia potest. Conati sunt plures inumbra sine lumine quaerere lucem, minime tamen potuerunt, quia sepultus iacet incineribus ignis. Nonnulli exercitati laruarum pictores, uentum unum in duos distinxerunt ad punctum, quorum alter misophos in tenebris latitat semper, alter uero lucis amator philosophos tenebras odit, lucem diligit, arcanum bubone custodit. Rursus Beda fuerunt constantennonulli,quorum intentio progrediens adlatiora, inuisibilem oculis uenium rebus colligabat uisibilibus, &; uegetabilia multa, nec minus lapides atq́; fructe ta, quae uocibus carent, lingua cogebat loqui humana. Quid inferam bruta,cum arti obtemperent cuncta? Hoc arcanum omnibus inuentis haec tenus iure praefertur, perquod occulta mysteriorum roburi Robur

[unclear] of monastic [unclear], previously a monster excessively wandering, at the sight of which no one could think what it was. Nor did the dissension of the owls come to rest before the image of the master had skillfully bound the magpie with a similar tetragon.

Marcus T. Cicero, an eloquent orator, using both natural talent and art, changed the small elements of phrasing into signs, and placed the careful mark, or character, of his intention in place of customary phrasing. Indeed he made use of such abundance in this very novelty that his invention could suffice for almost all things in the world. Moreover, to these heralds of mysteries the institution of the art gave marvelous agility, so that, beyond the nature of all things, solid and whole things might serve the good will of the master. A king can always make use of their service most safely, though not without great labor and manifest suspicion of the [unclear]. But Cyprian, most holy prelate and martyr of the church of Carthage, wishing to provide the very teachings of Ciceronian instruction for the use of Christians, enlarged them by no small degree, and added what had been lacking for our customs.

Pharamund also, the forty-third king of the Franks in Germany after Marcomer, most powerful, when in the year of the Lord’s nativity 424 he powerfully entered the borders of the Gauls, in order that everything might be done safely, bound foreign small elements to his secrets.

Clodius also, called Crinitus, the elder son, succeeding his father in the kingdom of the Franks, after he had violently subjected all Gaul to his rule, ordered all the Gauls, as conquered men and slaves, to be shorn and their beards shaved; but he commanded the Franks, conquerors and lords of the Gauls, to let their hair and beard grow. From this he was called Crinitus. In imitation of his father, he wrapped the mysteries of counsel in his own and foreign signs.

Charles, surnamed the Great, the sixty-third king of the Franks after Marcomer, who first of the Franks ruled over the Romans, with Nanno the grammarian as his teacher, wishing to adorn the German language, which was his native tongue, with grammarians after the model of Latin, began an arduous work, which nevertheless, entangled in many matters and overtaken by death, he did not complete. He bound owls with varied and many small elements; Brabant, or Namur in Germany, had no greater native than him. To the several prefects of the kingdom he gave, by art, individual owls. The Northmen, having come out from the borders of Gothia, when once they were cruelly devastating Gaul, summoned owls from Greece and prepared a safe hiding place for their secrets, which today is known to few.

Our Bede, a monk in England, not ignorant of the deed of the Northmen, described many inventions of the ancients similar to these, by which they made a path, bright with mysteries, dark. He was the first to commend artrology to the memory of posterity, and invented dactilogy. There were those who distinguished small elements by visible accidents; by their prudence night was turned into day, and without the service of owls light shone in darkness. Concerning these matters, the illustrious count palatine, prince elector, once an investigator of our Steganography, received from us a manifest experiment of the teaching.

But others, multiplying small elements by regulated division, after the manner of barbarians overturned the figures of nature, hiding in darkness the dances of the shadows of things coming into being; and where the secrecy of counsel required it, they supplied [perdiapyrana ta cabalam] to those absent.

Great labor is involved in these things, and a long exercise of the mind over many years, in which no one suddenly becomes skilled in practice. Necessity bears all things. There were also those whom heavenly harmony taught to compose foreign voices, of which there was a twofold use for those who understood, while one suspended the sense, the other [unclear] the mind. God can do all things. Many tried to seek light in shadow without light, yet they could not at all, because the fire lies buried in ashes. Some practiced painters of masks divided one wind into two to a point; one of them, a hater of light, always hides in darkness, while the other, a lover of light, a philosopher, hates darkness, loves light, and guards the secret with an owl. Again there were certain constant men of Bede, whose intention, advancing to broader things, bound an invisible vein to visible things before the eyes, and compelled many plants, and no less stones and fruits, which lack voices, to speak with a human tongue.

Why should I mention brute things, when all things obey art? This secret is rightly preferred to all discoveries up to now, through which the hidden things of mysteries [unclear]

Profunda in his latent mysteria,& paucis sunt manifesta· Amore breuitatis silentie plures praetererimus, qui naturam arte iuuantes, arcanis prudentiam adhibuerunt, &quod nescientibus multis uidebatur impossibile, sagaci studio inusum facilem produxerunt Culta mens grandia potest, & qui adhäret deo,intelligentia fit mundo altior· Multa sunt mysteria regum, & curis plenaconsilia in quibus confidẽtia requiritur et fides, quae rara nocet credenti et amp; dubium etiam cum adest, sapius admittit· Operaepretium idcirco fue=rit principes omnes philosophos esse, atque singulari praedit os sapientia,iustos, mansuetos, benevolos, & munificentia insignes, ut nec alios ipsiuelint uelint decipere, nec ab alijs facile queant supplantari. Sola prudentiae co mes iusticia, principem efficit gloriosum. Ad memorati principis, &amp; domini electoris Philippi Comitis palatini, Bauariaeque ducis instantiam, ego Ioannes Trithemius, nunc abbas monasterij sancti Iacobi apud Virci- burg, tunc uero diui Martini praesulis in Spanheim Moguntinae diocesis, octo mysteriorum libros in steganographia scribere coepi. Me autem in tertio iam libro eiusdem operis lucubrationem continuante, res contigit, quam breuiter si potero, sum dicturus. Anno dominicae natiuitatis mille- simo quadringentesimo nono, indictione Romanorum secun- da: sciscitanti per epistolam Arnoldo Bostio Carmelitae Gandauensis op= pidi, quid noui aederem, quibusue studijs occuparer, altera palmarum die per mercatores ut amico rescripsi, me habere sub incude nouum et amp; miran dum steganophiae opus, &amp; quid in singulis contineretur libris, per ordi nem reseraui. Verum prius quam epistola mea peruenisset Gandauũ, Bo- stius in diebus paschalibus è uita migrauit ad Christum. Cuius loci prior literas accepit, aperuit, legit, promissorumque nouitate (ut reor) attonitus, multis alijs rogantibus legendas et amp; rescribendas communicauit. Hinc est factum quod ipsa epistola mea, breui tempore per totam penè Germaniam et amp; Galliam diuulgata, saepiusque à pluribus rescripta, multos etiam doctissi mos uiros conuertit instuporem et amp; admirationem, usque adeo ut quid cum ueritate sentire deberẽt de me haefitarent. Ex his fuere nonnulli qui meas in dicta epistola pollicitationes constanter asseuerarent friuolas, impoßibi les, atque mendaces, &amp; à me inanis gloriae causa impudenter excogitatas. Alij uero dicebant: Magna et amp; miranda pollicetur iste abbas Trithe- mius, quae si potest, non aliter quam doemonum ministerio potest, cum na- turae metas procul uideantur excedere. Si uero non potest, quis eum dubi- tabit esse mendacem, &amp; ab omnibus uiris bonis et amp; doctis merito refutan- dum? Sed absit procul utrumque à me, quoniam naturalia promisi. Om- nium uero incognita mea temere iudicantium, maxime temerarius, &amp; ini- quißimus rerum aestimator tandem prorupit in medium, Carolus Bouillus, natione Picardus, qui cum superioribus partibus Alsatiae peragratis, ad ***

they take on strength and virtue. Yet reason bids one hide the great in small things, and by no means cast pearls before swine. From nothing, nothing is brought back. The visible multitude of things is known to be great, but invisible things remain remote from us; if these latter are prudently fitted to the former, the enlightened mind of man would know and behold wonders. But to treat further of these matters is not part of the present purpose; since they are greater and weightier, they require another work and another time.

Matthias, the most powerful king of Hungary and, harder than adamant, the hammer of the Turks, who in our age fought many victorious battles against the enemies of the cross of Christ, discovered many things by wondrous talent and art, adorned owls with circumlocutions, kept his own mysteries secret, concealed by manifold variety, and by manifest diligence destroyed the counsels of his enemies. He preferred wisdom to gold; therefore he always triumphed as a glorious victor. In a wise man there is a sound mind in a well-ordered body; when, borne upward by desire for higher understanding, you have returned through the likeness of the binary from the ternary into unity, thereafter it will now easily rise to the denary. Pythagoras of Samos, that philosopher, warned his disciples not to forget the quaternary, in which the first perfection of numbering is comprised. For thus we number: one, two, three, four. Halt your mind, for you have ten. The denary is the head of perfection. What are eleven, except ten and unity? What is twenty? Twice ten. What is forty? Four times ten. You have a hundred, and you have by no means departed from the quaternary. And what are a hundred, except ten times ten? Deep mysteries lie hidden in these things, and they are manifest to few.

For love of brevity we shall pass over many in silence, who, aiding nature by art, applied prudence to secret matters, and what seemed impossible to many who did not know, by keen study brought into easy use. A cultivated mind can do great things, and he who cleaves to God becomes, in understanding, higher than the world. There are many mysteries of kings, and counsels full of cares, in which trustworthiness and fidelity are required; when rare, this harms the believer, and even when doubt is present, it admits more often. Therefore it would be worthwhile for all princes to be philosophers, endowed with singular wisdom, just, gentle, benevolent, and distinguished for munificence, so that they themselves should neither wish to deceive others nor easily be able to be overthrown by others. Justice alone, the companion of prudence, makes a prince glorious.

At the urging of the aforesaid prince and lord elector Philip, count palatine and duke of Bavaria, I, Johannes Trithemius, now abbot of the monastery of Saint James at Wurzburg, but then of Saint Martin the bishop in Sponheim in the diocese of Mainz, began to write eight books of mysteries in steganography. But while I was already continuing my nocturnal labor on the third book of the same work, an event occurred which, if I can, I am going to recount briefly. In the year of the Lord's nativity one thousand four hundred [ninety-]nine, in the second Roman indiction, when Arnold Bostius, a Carmelite of the town of Ghent, asked by letter what new thing I was bringing forth, or with what studies I was occupied, on the day after Palm Sunday I wrote back through merchants, as to a friend, that I had under the hammer a new and wondrous work of steganography, and I disclosed in order what was contained in each of the books. But before my letter had reached Ghent, Bostius, in the days of Easter, departed from life to Christ. The prior of that place received the letter, opened it, read it, and, astonished, as I think, by the novelty of the things promised, shared it with many others who asked to read and copy it.

From this it happened that my letter itself, made known in a short time throughout almost all Germany and Gaul, and often copied by many, also turned very learned men to amazement and admiration, to such a degree that they hesitated what they ought truly to think of me. Among these there were some who steadfastly asserted that the promises I made in the said letter were frivolous, impossible, and false, and had been shamelessly devised by me for the sake of empty glory. Others, however, said: “This abbot Trithemius promises great and wondrous things; if he can do them, he can do so only by the ministry of demons, since they seem by far to exceed the bounds of nature. But if he cannot do them, who will doubt that he is a liar, and deservedly to be refuted by all good and learned men?” But let both be far from me, since I promised natural things. But of all those rashly judging things unknown to them about me, the most rash, and at last the most unjust appraiser of matters, came forth into the open: Charles de Bovelles, a Picard by nation, who, after travelling through the upper parts of Alsace, to

9
me gratia hospicij uenisset in Spanheim per Treuiros rediturus in Gal- liam, qua poteram humanitate ipsum tractaui, & omnia hospitalitatis be- neficia quamdiu mecum fuit hilari uultu exhibui. Cumque ut fieri solet inter amicos maximè literarum studiosos, omnia mea gratissimo hospiti exhi- buissem uidenda, cum alijs se obtulit etiam memoratum opus Steganogra- phiae necdum eo tempore consummatum. Vidit Bouillus, & obiter legit, mente aliunde occupatus se adinuentum mirari dixit, laudauit, nec quo in- telligeretur modo, curauit. Vnde cum non peteret intelligentiae clauem, nihil eorum quae continebantur in ipsa lucubratione nostra, meruit audire uel percipere. Reuersus post haec in Galliam, malum nobis pro bono red didit, & Christianae foedus amicitiae turpiter uiolauit. Interrogatus enim per dominum Germanum de Ganay, communem amicum, posteal episco- pum Aurelianensem, quid apud me reperisset, uidisseque in Spanheim, fal- sa proueris, & mendacia pro beneficijs rescripsit, damnans et temerè iu- dicans ea, quae compraehendere intellectu minimè ualebat. Nam cum doctri- nae sibi palmam inuidia et mendacio crederet fore conferendum, epistolam ad memoratum uirum doctißimum falsitate, mendacijs, iniurijs et contu- melijs multis plena rescripsit, in qua non intellectae Steganographiae mentio- nem faciens, me prauis artibus deditum, magum et necromanticum falso, mendaciter, & nimis iniuriose temeraria praesumptione procla- mat. Cuius mendacißimis iniurijs et blasphemijs, deo miserante, breuitas literarum responsurus, quo intelligat omnis posteritas et me innocentem, & Bouillum impium, crudelem, & temerarium esse in hac parte menda- cem. Constanter affirmo, ueraciter dico, et confidenter in animam mea iu- ro, cum demonibus, prauis aut perniciosis, magicis uel necromaticis arti- bus me nullum unquam habuisse commertium: sed omnia et singula, quae uel scripst, uel scripturum me sum pollicitus, purae esse, sana, naturalia, & Christianae fidei in nullo penitus aduersa. Vnde non uereor mea pro- missa coram uiris bonis et doctis, quando et quotiens opus fuerit, dare ex- amina, quorum determinationi nullatenus intendo reluctari. Quod hanc Bouillanae temeritatis historiam huic praefationi meae interposui, causara tiona tienabilis fuit, ut intelligant omnes maturo factum consilio, quod hactenus manet in tenebris opus steganographiae sepultum, non quod temeraria Bo uilli iudicia metuam: sed ne causam pluribus uidear dare similibus de me si= milia suspicandi Enimuero quantum ad me attinet, mallem aemulos meos placare silentio, quam literis irritare uel scripturis ad insaniam prouoca=re.Satius enim iudicaui, omnia mirabiliter inventa perpetuo damnare si=lentio, quam magicae uel necromanticae perniciosae superstitionis notam, falsa etiam hominum aestimatione incurrere.Lateat ergo steganographia in tenebris,nec fiat Bouillinae societati mēdaci communis,quae de rebus iu=dicare consueuit incognitis, &; deprauare famam boni uiꝑi sola libidine prauitatis.Veruntamen cohortantibus amicis, ut cum Bouillo intelligant aemuli nostri quam temeratam et ementitam nobis iniuriam fecerit (ma=nente suis in terminis Steganographia) subiectum opus, quod Polygra= phiam nuncupamus,per sex libros distinctum,in lucem edere consenti=mus. Legant qui uolunt,&; sine stomacho legant hoc volumen amici,cu=ius cū latentia mysteria intellexerint omnia,ipsi absque inuidia sint iudices,naturalia sint an superstitiosa.Scio enim et certus sum omnia esse syn=eera,pura,naturalia,et ab omni studio superstitionis malae remota.Quotiens autem sermo pręcedit obscurior,eae fit ratione, ne gladio de fensionis uesanus abuteretur ad interitum, quem animo et mente sanus ad sui defert munimentum.Nihil tamē propterea in eo continetur mali,cum bonis etiam rebus in malum abutantur peruersi.Quisquis autem hanc aedi=tionem nostram condemnare praesumpserit, ipse sibi conscius est et te=stis, quod eam nunquam ueraciter intellexit.Celantur sub enigmatibus mysteria,ne bacuceis fiant bubonum arcana quomodolibet manifesta.Si quem haec scire delectat,remota procul inuidia lector accedat.Sum etenim Christianus,sum presbyter sub norma diui patris Benedicti et monachus,Christū diligo,et qua possum synceritate mentis deuotus semper adoro,nulla mihi sunt,nulla fuerunt,et protectore Deo nulla erunt cūdemonibus commertia,nulla inmagicis,seu profanis artibus studia,nulle documenta. Qui de me aliter sentit,***) ij

had come to me at Spanheim as a guest, intending to return to France through Trier, I treated him with all the courtesy I could, and as long as he was with me I showed him every benefit of hospitality with a cheerful countenance. And when, as is usual among friends, especially those devoted to letters, I had shown all my things to my most welcome guest for him to see, among the rest the aforementioned work of Steganography, not yet completed at that time, also presented itself. Bovillus saw it and read it in passing, with his mind occupied elsewhere; he said that he wondered at the invention, praised it, and took no care to understand in what manner it was to be understood. Hence, since he did not ask for the key of understanding, he deserved to hear or perceive nothing of what was contained in that lucubration of ours. After this, having returned to France, he repaid us evil for good and shamefully violated the bond of Christian friendship. For when he was asked by Lord Germain de Ganay, a common friend, later bishop of Orleans, what he had found with me and seen at Spanheim, he wrote back falsehoods as truths and lies in return for benefits, condemning and rashly judging things that he was quite unable to comprehend with his understanding. For since, through envy and falsehood, he believed that the palm of learning would be conferred upon him, he wrote back to the aforementioned most learned man a letter full of falsity, lies, injuries, and many insults, in which, making mention of the Steganography that he had not understood, he falsely, mendaciously, and very injuriously proclaims me, by rash presumption, to be given over to wicked arts, a magician and necromancer. To his most mendacious injuries and blasphemies, God having mercy, the brevity of letters will respond, so that all posterity may understand both that I am innocent and that Bovillus is impious, cruel, rash, and a liar in this matter. I affirm steadfastly, I speak truthfully, and I swear confidently upon my soul that I have never had any commerce with demons, or with wicked or pernicious, magical or necromantic arts; but that all and every thing that I have either written or promised that I would write are pure, sound, natural, and in no respect at all contrary to the Christian faith. Hence I do not fear to give my promised things for examination before good and learned men, whenever and as often as there shall be need, and I do not in any way intend to resist their determination. The reason why I inserted this history of Bovillus's rashness into this preface of mine was reasonable, so that everyone may understand that it was done by mature counsel that the work of Steganography has hitherto remained buried in darkness, not because I fear the rash judgments of Bovillus, but lest I seem to give occasion to many similar persons to suspect similar things of me. Indeed, as far as I am concerned, I would rather placate my rivals by silence than irritate them by letters or provoke them to madness by writings. For I judged it better to condemn all wonderfully invented things to perpetual silence than, even by the false opinion of men, to incur the mark of magical or necromantic pernicious superstition. Therefore let Steganography lie hidden in darkness, and let it not become common to the lying fellowship of Bovillus, which is accustomed to judge matters unknown to it and to deprave the reputation of a good man by the mere lust of depravity. Nevertheless, at the urging of friends, so that our rivals may understand, together with Bovillus, how rash and lying an injury he has done us, while the Steganography remains within its own bounds, we consent to publish the following work, which we call Polygraphy, divided into six books. Let those who wish read it, and let friends read this volume without resentment; when they have understood all its hidden mysteries, let them themselves be judges, without envy, whether they are natural or superstitious. For I know and am certain that all things are sincere, pure, natural, and far removed from every pursuit of evil superstition. Whenever, however, the discourse is rather obscure, this is done for the reason that a madman should not abuse to destruction the sword of defense which a man sound in mind and intellect carries for his own protection. Yet nothing evil is contained in it on that account, since perverse men abuse even good things for evil. But whoever presumes to condemn this edition of ours is himself conscious and a witness to himself that he has never truly understood it. Mysteries are concealed under enigmas, lest the secrets of [unclear] should in any way be made manifest to owls. If it delights anyone to know these things, let the reader approach with envy put far away. For I am a Christian, I am a priest, and a monk under the rule of the divine father Benedict; I love Christ, and with whatever sincerity of mind I can I always devoutly adore him. I have no dealings with demons, I have had none, and, with God as protector, I shall have none; no studies in magical or profane arts, no teachings. Whoever thinks otherwise of me,

10
male sentit, iniuriam facit, & apertum Bouilli mendacium defendit. Sed iam nunc ista missa faciamus, & quid in unoquoque polygraphiae nostrae libro contineatur, per ordinem enarremus. [unclear] PINAX SIVE INDEX EORVM QVAe in primo libro tractantur. IN primo huius Polygraphiae nostrae libri dictiones latini sermonis, quotquot cernuntur, per ordinem ternarij nostri locantes distribuimus: quarium usu et ministerio cuncti per orbem principes in quibuslibet ar- canis tutum reperient obsequium, quod sine periculo mysterij, sine notꝫ, &amp; sine suspitione bacuceorum, perpetuo manebit occultum. Bubonibus constat his iter tutum, &amp; nulla unquam indagatione cuiusquam uiolan- dum. Duobus tantum scientia rei latentis conceditur, si binarius scite ad monadem reuocetur. Ignorantia est mater erroris, &amp; qui bonum discere contemnit quod nescit amat caecitatem. Sunt autem ipsa periphrasmata in modum porrecta uel monentis, uel supplicantis, quae ad omnem huius mun di visibilem possunt materiam uariari. Singulis enim sunt apta mysterijs, &amp; Graecorũ non secus ac nostris praeponuntur arcanis, cum ea intellexeris quae uides, non temere contemnas latentia quae non uides. Accidentia cer= nis, substantia manet invisibilis. Vnde maiora latent, minora intuentibus patent. Quod cum ratione sit factum, nemo uir bonus in malum recipiat, cū omnibus idoneus ex his ad altiora posset, modo uelit, proficere. Mihi au tem hac uice non placuit altiora in lucem profundere, cum importunum tempus uideatur obuiare. Latini alphabeti litteras per ordinem singulis dictionibus ea consyderatione praeposito, quatenus et amp; operator modum ha beat in proposito facilem, &amp; reciprocus in relatione à labore nimio releue tur. Paraphrasmata quae positam sunt extra rectum ordinem linearum, Bubonibus [unclear] non uacant à mysterio artis, quoniam lucifluis deservunt propositionibus ad perfectionis necessariae consumationem, non opacis. Propterea quoque assumuntur in illis, negliguntur in istis. Ipsa enim certa sunt media quibus tollitur omnis suspicio adversantis. Omnia ratione sunt posita, ut nec una quidë ppositio introducatur ociofa. Quanto exempli gratia, sol ab aequinoctiali circulo plus progreeditur, tanto habitantibus in illis regionibus dies prolongantur. Propterea ut unitas ordine recto progrediatur mediante ternario in binarium, paradigma quod tradimus, est diligentius obseruandum. Et primo quidem intentionis sue operator intelligens con sideratione praehabita, quid ternario per binarium sit concessurus animaduertat, diem cum nocte per minuta diuidat, uentorumque minutias, non aliena sed propria phraseos suppositione distinguat. In quolibet negotio mystico diligentemente caeuat, ne constitutum artis peruertat ordinem, nec paraphrasmatum alterum supponat pro altero, nec uni concedat alteri debitum, aliocquin unitas binarium non admittit, eritque confusa et inutilis operatio tota. Non sit nimia prolixitate nox uaga, non progredivs instablis ultra constitutos arte sibi terminos, non aquam curiositas permutet in niuem, nec dormiat in die qui noctem uigilat. Mens ingenio follicita, utatur et arte ne manus committat sua leuitate errorem, qui modicus et paruus in monade, multus semper et maximus in binario consueuit ap parere. Vnum de quolibet ordine paraphrasma, in ministerium arcani duntaxat admittitur, cui seruitoris exemplo, quotiens luminis particula diei expostulauerit, phrasis una similiter subhaerens, non plures assumuntur. Haec animo sunt commendanda uigilanti, cauendumque ne uentus anime tur. Norma post haec praescribitur accedenti artis ad practicam, ut unam hominis persona ex duabus constantè naturis, anima scilicet uisibilia supe rante, et carne uisibili manente, quantũ praeuaelet arte mystica imitetur. Nam sicuti anima non uidetur, licet in corpore sit constituta uisibili, ita mentis arcanum ut secretum maneat, & operetur nihilominus ad placi tum, luminis ductum requirit, perdurans in suo ergasterio tenebrarum. Quotiens ergo ministrat animae corpus, domino seruus, rationi uoluntas *** ii

he thinks wrongly, does injury, and defends Bovillus’s open falsehood. But now let us set those matters aside, and recount in order what is contained in each book of our Polygraphia.

TABLE, OR INDEX OF THE THINGS THAT ARE TREATED IN THE FIRST BOOK.

In the first book of this Polygraphia of ours we arrange and distribute the words of the Latin language, as many as are visible, placing them according to the order of our ternary; by the use and service of these, all princes throughout the world will find, in any secrets whatever, a secure assistance, which, without danger to the mystery, without [unclear], and without suspicion of [unclear], will remain forever hidden. With these owls the journey is secure, and never to be violated by any investigation of anyone. Knowledge of the hidden matter is granted to two only, if the binary is skillfully brought back to the monad. Ignorance is the mother of error, and he who scorns to learn the good which he does not know loves blindness. These periphrases themselves are extended in the manner either of one advising or of one entreating, and they can be varied for every visible subject of this world. For they are suited to individual mysteries, and are set before the secrets of the Greeks no less than before our own; when you have understood the things you see, do not rashly despise the hidden things which you do not see. You perceive the accidents; the substance remains invisible. Hence the greater things lie hidden, while the lesser are open to those who look upon them. Since this has been done with reason, let no good man take it for evil, since from these every suitable person could advance to higher things, provided he wished to do so. But to me, at this turn, it has not seemed good to pour forth the higher things into the light, since an unfavorable time seems to stand in the way. I have set the letters of the Latin alphabet in order before the individual words with this consideration: that the operator may have an easy method in what he has set before him, and that the reciprocal correspondent may be relieved from excessive labor in the relation. The paraphrases which have been placed outside the straight order of the lines,

Consequenter item monemus uolen= tem, ut quotiens à uento mouetur folium, utriusque proprietatem naturae discernat, ipsamque noctem diei per gradus &; minuta comparet, ac luci te= nebras conformet. Quod si phoebus nocti, aut nox praeiudicauerit soli, per quod eclipseos confusionasceretur, aut unitas resumat binarium, quem di misit in lumine, aut umbra noctis ad primam reducatur lineam solis. Cum ergo memoratae difficultatis nodum incideris, minutias nu mera noctis, paraphrasmata quoque nota diurni luminis, &; sic alterum ex altero distempera, ut sequatur actioni proportio necessaria. Caue ne du= rante solis eclipsi, necessarium intermittas laborem. Quam ob causam non interroges, cum scias nihil in mundo esse tam bonum &; sanctum, quo reprobi non sae pius abutantur in malum. EORVM QVAe IN SECVNDO Polygraphiae libro tractantur indicium. IN secundo Polygraphiae libro, nihil à primo noui componitur, in quo so lius dici paraphrasmata uariantur. Propterea quicquid obseruandum in illo diximus, etiam in isto custodiendum fore admonemus. Mutantur etiam ad placi- tum feronomata, si quando conuertantur ad gradus integros minuta. Quo facto confurget in arte mirabile opus per omnia, & stabit imagine pro- ductus in lumine mundus, & non erit in operante bacuceorum pauor ullus. Faciem rebus his potuissem induxisse pulchriorem, si aut spe aliqua lu- cri, aut propriae utilitatis usu, ut ea scriberem inductus acceßissem. Sed cum nihil horum me induxerit ad scribendum, satis uidebatur cupientibus occasionem dedisse, atque materiam nostris inuentis politiora superaddere, & artem arte uenustare. EORVM QVAe IN TER- tio Polygraphiae libro continen tur indicium. IN tertio Polygraphiae libro fines praescriptae nationis nostrae consilio rationis transgreßi, ad peregrina ducimur, & in medio Francorum essentialiter constituti, per imagines et similitudines barbarorum longius euagamur. Quatuor enim ferè milibus mythologicis arte phrasmatibus in ordinem collocatis, uiam unitati artificiali nimis facilem ostendimus, per quam symbolicas notiones binario suo com- municabit omni tempore securus. Durior hic est unitate binarius, & nisi philologus noster prudentia fit occulatus, monadi binarium reddet contra- rium. Nam solus ternarius, qui ab unitate binarioq́; procedit, tanquam palidromus in se connectit utrumque. Quod si rationis necessariae utili- tas, ultra propositae rei metas extenditur, toties paraphrasmata per mi- nutias à die principio numerentur, donec minuta constituant gradum in quo nox aequatur diei. Facies imaginis huius perpetuum nouit si- lentium, nec fraudes metuit bacuceorum. Quanta uolueris copia exten- ditur, & sine numero uariatur. INDICVLVS SIVE PINA- cion eorum quae tractantur in li- bro quarto

[They] are not devoid of the mystery of the art, because they serve luminous propositions, necessary for the consummation of the requisite perfection, not obscure ones. For this reason also they are taken up in the former and neglected in the latter. For they themselves are sure means by which every suspicion of opposition is removed. All things have been set down by reason, so that not even one proposition is introduced idly. By way of example: the farther the sun advances from the equinoctial circle, by so much are the days lengthened for those dwelling in those regions. Therefore, so that unity may advance in the right order, through the mediation of the ternary, into the binary, the paradigm which we hand down must be observed rather diligently. And first indeed let the operator, understanding his intention, after prior consideration, attend to what he is going to grant to the ternary through the binary; let him divide the day together with the night into minutes, and distinguish the minute portions of the winds, not by a foreign but by the proper supposition of the phrase. In any mystical business let him diligently beware lest he overturn the established order of the art, or substitute one paraphrasm for another, or grant to one what is owed to another; otherwise unity does not admit the binary, and the whole operation will be confused and useless. Let the night not wander in excessive prolixity, not advancing unstably beyond the limits established for it by the art; let curiosity not change water into snow, nor let him sleep by day who keeps vigil by night. Let the mind, solicitous in its talent, use art also, lest the hand by its own levity commit an error, which, though slight and small in the monad, is accustomed always to appear great and very large in the binary. One paraphrasm from each order is admitted only into the service of the secret; following its servant’s example, as often as a small particle of the light of day shall demand it, one phrase similarly adhering, not several, is taken up. These things must be entrusted to a watchful mind, and care must be taken lest the wind be stirred.

After these things a rule is prescribed for one approaching the practice of the art: that he imitate, as far as he can by the mystical art, the one person of man, consisting steadfastly of two natures, namely the soul surpassing visible things and the flesh remaining visible. For just as the soul is not seen, although it is established in a visible body, so the secret of the mind, in order that it may remain secret and nevertheless operate at pleasure, requires the guidance of light, while enduring in its workshop of shadows. Therefore as often as the body ministers to the soul, the servant to the master, the will to reason, see that the principal virtue of the power in the light of the paraphrasm is preserved in its natural vigor. For by this instruction the first of the Peripatetics will duly enter upon the second, and the monad will enter the binary. Consequently we likewise admonish the willing man that, as often as a leaf is moved by the wind, he should discern the property of each nature, compare the night itself with the day by degrees and minutes, and conform the shadows to the light. But if Phoebus should prejudice the night, or night the sun, through which a confusion of eclipse would arise, either let unity resume the binary which it dismissed in the light, or let the shadow of night be brought back to the first line of the sun.

Hold fixed in memory whatever is produced anywhere in number, weight, and measure. Therefore, when you have cut into the knot of the difficulty mentioned, number the minute portions of the night, note also the paraphrasms of the daylight, and so temper one from the other that the necessary proportion may follow the action. Beware lest, while the eclipse of the sun lasts, you interrupt the necessary labor. Attend no less that you be mindful of the ancient fathers, Tuisco, who, the grandson of Noah, is the father of the Teutons, and Marcomer, who is read to have been the first to lead the people of the Franks from the borders of Scythia into Germany, to the mouths of the Rhine. For the Franks are brothers of the Greeks and, intermingled with the Germans, once made two languages from one. Hence, according to the oracle .g.gg., those who lost one g. take it up. You are warned, zealous investigator of the newest Polygraphy, that after, eager as you are for the water of these inventions, you have obtained the true mode of operating, you should guard all things prudently and not pour them out indiscriminately into the knowledge of all men, especially filthy ones. For this reason do not ask, since you know that there is nothing in the world so good and holy that the wicked do not rather often abuse it for evil.

An indication of the things treated in the second book of the Polygraphy.

In the second book of the Polygraphy, nothing new is composed apart from the first, in which only the paraphrasms of speech are varied. Therefore we admonish that whatever we said must be observed in that book must also be kept in this one. For the symbols of both books have been composed under the path of light in the same [unclear] and order:

Aliud hîc latet incortice, & aliud reperitur in communi signo- rum operatione. Nam sicuti spiritus in sanguine corpus humanum uiuificat, ita uigor latens in arte operationem commendat. Propterea cuicunque huius inuenti cognitio est necessaria, oculos intellectus ape- riat, ut quae sit operationis cuiuslibet proprietas, comprehendat. Sic enim cupimus bonis uiris omnia esse peruia, ut si fieri posset, nunquam tamen reprobis fierent manifesta. Quae tamen nouitas, ut sine rationabili causa non fieret pu- blica sub incubitis numerandi signis et notis mysticè fuerat occultanda. Semper enim uenti nocturnales diurnis sunt fortiores, & sicuti nox diem ordine suo intercipit, sic lumen tenebras exhorrescit. Quod natura ne- gat, nemo foeliciter audet. Rogamus lectorem, ne hoc laboriosum opus nostrum contemnet priuꝰ quam intelligat, sed iudex sine temeritate ut esse queat, corticem prudenter amoueat, quatenus ad nucleum latentem per- ueniat. Bonum et naturale est opus, quod ad bonum conuerti potest usum uel malum, pro ut uniuscunque mouetur desiderium uoluntatis. Bonum instrumentum est gladius, ad usum quoque bonum conuertitur, quotiens pro defensione sine iniuria portatur. placed, and with only the meaning of the paraphrasmata necessarily changed. In both, according to the capacity of human talent, multiple progressions can be made, since the words are varied by metathesis. The [feronomata] too are changed at will, whenever minutes are converted into whole degrees. When this has been done, a work altogether wonderful in the art will arise, and the world, brought forth by an image, will stand in the light, and there will be no fear at all of the Bacuceans in the one who is operating. I could have given these matters a more beautiful face, if I had been induced to write them by some hope of profit or by the use of my own advantage. But since none of these things induced me to write, it seemed enough to have given those who desired it an occasion and material to add more polished things to our inventions, and to adorn art by art.

An indication of the things that are contained in the third book of the Polygraphia.

In the third book of the Polygraphia, having by a reasoned plan overstepped the bounds of our prescribed nation, we are led to foreign things, and, being essentially set in the midst of the Franks, we wander farther abroad through images and likenesses of barbarians. For with nearly four thousand mythological phrasmata arranged in order by art, we show a very easy way to artificial unity, through which it will at all times safely communicate symbolic notions to its binary. Here the binary is harder than unity, and unless our philologist is sharp-sighted with prudence, he will make the binary contrary to the monad. For only the ternary, which proceeds from unity and the binary, as a palindrome joins both together in itself. But if the usefulness of necessary reason is extended beyond the limits of the proposed matter, let the paraphrasmata be counted each time by minutes from the beginning of the day, until the minutes establish the degree in which night is equal to day. The face of this image knows perpetual silence and does not fear the deceits of the Bacuceans. It is extended in as great an abundance as you wish, and is varied without number.

Brief index or table of the things that are treated in the fourth book.

In the fourth book of the Polygraphia we place much confidence in the binary, which, with all obstacles removed, without the labor of difficulty, at first sight we have reduced to unity. Hence here we use a circle in great things, a line or point in the smallest things. Nor does it matter if night exceeds day, or if light does not agree with darkness, because the circle does not receive an end, and fullness does not admit a void. For they are contraries, and whenever they succeed one another, one is corrupted by the other. A singular mystery assisting the binary is handed down in this fourth book of the Polygraphia, since the airy wind itself, the composer of the base, is never designated in anything other than the binary. But in that part the lightness of the owls is always suspect to us in difficult matters. The construction of this thing makes paraphrasmata with infinite atoms.

Index or table of the things that are treated in the fifth book.

In the fifth book of the Polygraphia, we have inscribed in order on two tables the letters of the Latins, which we Germans also use; one of these is called the straight table, while the other is named the reverse. Beneath these we have placed windy dances, so that what we seek with labor among foreign things we may see among our own without difficulty. For besides those things that have been set down by us openly, many other secret things still lie hidden within, through the understanding of which a path is opened for the operator toward greater things, though these are by no means proposed to all. We have also set letters beneath numbers, by which hidden things may be made manifest at our will. Hence through the skilled operation of this book, all messages are safely handed on to the cabalists, although the mysteries are not free from suspicion of the Bacuceans. For every form of metathesis of signs produces suspicion in the observer, although it brings no harm to the owls. But you, who have attained the understanding of this work, will easily penetrate every metathesis of letters among our countrymen and the Latins.

Prima utilitas est , quod consummata huius operis intelligentia modum dat facitem , quo mentis tuae arcanum tuto , secretè , ac sine aliqua suspitione quorumcunq ; intuentium notum facies industri am scienti quam latissimè fuerit opus ad quamlibet locorum distantiam sermone regulatam .
