Secunda utilitas est , qu od ministerio hui us operis in parui temporis spacio , hominem latina sermonis ignarum , modo literas tantum legere ac scribere nouerit sub lingua materna , docebis sub latina lingu a ut uolueris , ornate uel concinne scribere , omnia q; uoluntatis suae arca na mysteria celare , abscondere , artemq́; scienti quam placuerit , latissimè nunciare tuto , secret è , et absq ; suspitione . Iterum praemoneo , ne aliter nos intelliga s pollicitos quam pollicemur . Tertia uero utilitas , quod Roma ni sermonis imperitum , non solum in paucis doceb is horis quod polic licenyr, Licemur, scribere, de legere, sed etiam intelligere, si prudenter munus offi= cij adhibueris, quod non sine rationabili causanos duximus reserandum. Scribet enim artis nouae discipulus quam non nouerat linguam, & latinum Sermonem sub institutione regulata compositum, intelliget interpretabiturq́;, si iusseris ipse de uerbũ. Denique ad omnes muni di res atque negocia haec institutio potest ampliari Quemadmodum ista fie ri poterint si quis ex me scire uoluerit inprimis talem se praestare meminerit, ut accipere mereatur Non enim omnia debentur omnibus, sed alter est alteri praeferendus. Quarta utilitas est quod per ampliationem similitudinis rei acceptae, omnia ista in quamlibet possunt linguam extendi, reducto instituente binario ad unitatem. Quod tamen haud paßim quilibet hominum potest, sed ille tantum quem deo praeueniente sua gratia speciali, ars et natura dignificarunt. Quinta utilitas, quod imitatione similitudinis communicare possumus artem inuentionis nostrae scienti que mentisque quantuncunque voluerimus abunde, multipliciter, & latissimè, varijs modis, qui ab alio nullo poterunt sciri uel notari. Datur istic multiplex sine uoce locutio, per quam tuto, securè, latißimè, omni suspitione remota, mentis nostrae conceptiones uniuersas, quantumlibet arduas, scientibus artem plenissime indicare poterimus. Et haec inventio miranda progressiones habet innumerabiles, omniumque mysteriorum capaces. Sexta utilitas est, quod per intelligentiam huius operis qualibet methatesin siue transpositionem literarũ regulatam inuenire poteris, easq́; nihilominus sic formare, quod solis noscentibus artem, & alteri penitus nulli subseruint in mundo. Et magna uis est metatheseos formae, simul et operationis, quae et plures habet modos, & multipliciter variatur. Septima utilitas est, quod par intelligentiam huius uoluminis maxima datur facultas cupientibus ad ampliandam sine labore memoriam, quotiens minutiarum semina debitis gradibus collocantur. Omnia propter causam bonitatis latent arcanis uerborum atque figurarum inuoluta, quae si quis intelligere plenius optauerit, reuocet in mentem, quoniam labor improbus omnia uincit. Mihi etenim satis fuerit artis inuenisse principia, *** ij

A Little Index, or Table, of the things contained in the sixth book

In the sixth book, which is the last book of our Polygraphia, once mental narration has been introduced, we have set forth in order the minute details of almost all the preceding signs and degrees, and with arithmetical distributions we have brought the functions of the letters into the service of cabalistic operation. One thing lies hidden here in the bark, and another is found in the common operation of the signs. For just as the spirit in the blood gives life to the human body, so the vigor hidden in the art commends the operation. Therefore whoever needs knowledge of this invention should open the eyes of his understanding, so that he may comprehend what is the property of each operation. For we desire all things to be open to good men in such a way that, if it were possible, they should nevertheless never become manifest to the reprobate. A reason compelled us to fit the letters of the Latins to numbers, lest, if we were too obscure, the intention of our mind should be clear to no one. Yet this novelty, so that it should not become public without reasonable cause, had to be hidden mystically under [unclear] signs and marks of numbering. For nocturnal winds are always stronger than diurnal ones, and just as night overtakes day in its order, so light shudders at darkness. What nature denies, no one happily dares. We ask the reader not to despise this laborious work of ours before he understands it, but, so that he may be a judge without rashness, let him prudently remove the bark, in order to reach the hidden kernel. Good and natural is a work that can be turned to good use or bad, according as the desire of each person’s will is moved. A sword is a good instrument, and is turned also to good use whenever it is carried for defense without injury. But if it is directed unjustly to the wounding of anyone, through abuse a good thing is loosened into evil. Therefore, so that the good may have something by which they may prudently provide for their affairs, the Polygraphia is written by us; and, lest an occasion for wrongdoing be furnished to the depraved, the kernel is hidden in the bark under various enigmas. He who is good does not abuse a good thing for evil; rather, if he can, he turns evil into good.

What are the causes of this work of ours, the Polygraphia, together with its advantages

We have undertaken the labor of the present work, both rare and arduous, for no other reason than that we might provide for the usefulness of those in need. I say those in need, not of food, not of drink, but of assistance in preserving secrets without danger. Therefore we judge it worthwhile if we briefly note the uses and advantages that can come to those who use these inventions of ours. Indeed, since in our own domestic affairs we have no business such that we need these teachings for concealing secrets, we have certainly labored for those whose command had to be obeyed. The first advantage is that, when understanding of this work is complete, it gives an easy method by which you will make the secret of your mind known safely, secretly, and without any suspicion on the part of any observers, to one who knows the art, as widely as need shall be, across any distance of places, by regulated speech.

What lies hidden in these things the work of steganography draws out, which requires neither letters nor a messenger who knows the secrets he is to carry. It would be otherwise in matters that admit the light, according to the common custom of all our people. Do not take the matter otherwise than it is. The second advantage is that, through the service of this work, in a short space of time you will teach a man ignorant of the Latin tongue, provided only that he knows how to read and write letters under his mother tongue, to write under the Latin language as you wish, ornately or neatly, and to conceal all the secret mysteries of his will, and to announce, safely, secretly, and without suspicion, the art to one who knows it, as widely as he pleases. Again I warn you beforehand not to understand us as having promised otherwise than we promise. The third advantage, however, is that you will teach one unskilled in the Roman tongue, not only in a few hours what [unclear],

Nam ut cultiora nostra formarentur inuenta, nec tempus erat, nec ratio, ne mel nauseantibus uomitum, aut ueritas odium pareret indignantibus. Omne tempus suis appreciandum est meritis, &; porci non sunt unionibus exornandi, nec preciosis onustandi margaritis. Importuna sunt omnia, quae moribus &; temporii non concordant mortalium qui bus ingeruntur. Multa fuerunt ingenia hominum nobilißima temporibus alienis, &; plura inueniuntur noua quotidiè ferme temporibus non proprijs. Quid egregio uertificatori Bartholo sub Innocentio Papa octauo conduxit nauticae artis miranda inuentio, quam in quodam libello uenalem ducatis centum milibus pollicetur, cum nec ipse pontifex summus, nec Veneti, nec Ianuenses, quibus rem suam proposuit emendam pro modico saltem cum illo dignarentur conuenire? Mensibus enim tri ginta nauem arte sua in medio maris posse seruare illaesam, resarcire fraetam, atque proiecta quaeque in profundum, sine periculo reuocare promisit. Sed nemo curauit Nec me fugit multos cum Nasone ingenio perisse suo. Satius est igitur scientiae ponere modum, quam sine fructu se odio &; detractioni exponere multorum, quibus familiarius est scientiam quam libet contemnere, quam didicisse. Quicquid enim nocere potest uulgatum, mystico fuerat sermone rationa- biliter occultandum. Materia uerò quam in Polygraphia tractamus, ad reipublicae commodum inter uiros bonos multum est bona, utilis et amp; hone- sta, quàm idcirco rationabili causa persuasi cōscripsimus, ut eius ministerio bonos homines in suis arcans alterutrum nunciandis tutos et securos à pra uorū inuestigatione redderemus. Verū ne prauis atque peruerfis, qui bonis etiā frequētius abutuntur inuentis, occasio praeberetur decipiēdi simplicio res, minufsque cautos in aestimatione rerū, modos in ea scribendi mysticos tra didimus fiue occultos, latentemque in medulla ueritatem tegumentis quibus dam operuimus figurarū. Licet minimè dubitemus uirū quēlibet industriū, istarunque rerū desiderio cupidū, facilè capturum omnia, si uel modicam in perscrutando adhibuerit continuationē Neque enim tam ardua, neque tan tis funt mysterijs inuoluta quae tradidi, ut à uiro studiofo penitus nequeāt penetrari. Sic enim ubique temperauimus dictionū nostrarū aenigmata, quo et doctis studiosisq́; uiris de facili fint peruia, et pigris tenebrionibus nihil ominus permaneat inacceffa. Verū posteaquā ipfum polygraphiae opus [unclear]

We are permitted not only to write and to read, but also to understand, if you have prudently applied the duty of the office, which we have thought should be disclosed not without reasonable cause. For the pupil of the new art will write a language which he did not know, and will understand and interpret Latin discourse composed under regulated instruction, if you yourself command him word by word. Finally, this instruction can be extended to all the things and affairs of the world. If anyone wishes to learn from me how these things can be done, let him remember first of all to show himself such that he deserves to receive it. For not all things are owed to all people, but one person is to be preferred to another.

The fourth usefulness is that, through the enlargement of the likeness of the thing received, all these things can be extended into any language whatever, with the instituting binary reduced to unity. Yet not just anyone among men can do this everywhere, but only he whom, with God going before him by his special grace, art and nature have made worthy.

The fifth usefulness is that, by imitation of likeness, we can communicate the art of our invention to one who knows it, and as much as we wish of our mind, abundantly, in many ways, and very widely, by various methods, which cannot be known or observed by anyone else. Here is given a manifold speech without voice, by which, safely, securely, very widely, with all suspicion removed, we shall be able to indicate fully to those who know the art all the conceptions of our mind, however difficult. And this wonderful invention has innumerable progressions, capable of all mysteries.

The sixth usefulness is that, through understanding this work, you will be able to discover any regulated metathesis or transposition of letters, and nevertheless to form them in such a way that they serve only those who know the art, and absolutely no one else in the world. And great is the power of metathesis in its form and also in its operation, which both has many modes and is varied in many ways.

The seventh usefulness is that, through understanding this volume, a very great faculty is given to those who desire to enlarge the memory without labor, whenever the seeds of minutiae are set in their proper degrees. All things, for the sake of goodness, lie hidden, wrapped in the secrets of words and figures; if anyone wishes to understand them more fully, let him recall to mind that unremitting labor conquers all things. For it will have been enough for me to have discovered the principles of the art and to have handed down a rough method of writing, and one intentionally unformed. For there was neither time nor reason for our discoveries to be shaped in a more polished form, lest honey produce vomiting in the nauseated, or truth produce hatred in the indignant. Every age is to be valued according to its own merits, and swine are not to be adorned with pearls, nor loaded with precious jewels. All things are untimely which do not agree with the habits and times of the mortals upon whom they are thrust. There have been many very noble talents among men in unsuitable times, and more new ones are found almost daily in times not their own. What advantage did the wonderful invention of nautical art bring to the excellent [versifier?] Bartholus under Pope Innocent VIII, which in a certain little book he offered for sale for one hundred thousand ducats, when neither the supreme pontiff himself, nor the Venetians, nor the Genoese, to whom he proposed that his invention be bought, deigned even to meet with him for a small amount? For he promised that by his art he could keep a ship unharmed in the middle of the sea for thirty months, repair one that was broken, and bring back without danger whatever had been cast into the deep. But no one cared. Nor has it escaped me that many, with Naso, have perished by their own genius. It is therefore better to set a limit to knowledge than to expose oneself fruitlessly to the hatred and detraction of many, for whom it is more familiar to despise any knowledge whatever than to have learned it.

End of the Preface

On the seventh day of April, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1508.

OMnis intentio nostra in toto Polygraphiae opere circa eam uersatur sententiam, qua modos traderemus certos occultè scribēdi, perquos reges et principes, nobiles et ignobiles, sacerdotes et laici, docti simul et indocti, secretè, tuto, & sine ulla suspitione latentis arcani, sibi mutuo et quibuslibet amicis, etiam longè ab inuicem distantibus, ministerio literarum quicquid et quotiens opus fuerit mentium suarum queant nunciare conceptum. Quod ne uel primi uel soli praesumpsisse ui deamur deamur deamur praemonemus lectorem plures olim ueterum, maximè tyrannos, principes et reges simili consyderatione motos, familiares sibi ac ua- rios excogitauisse modos et canones scribendi, quibus id quod uniuersali ter in polygraphia nostra sumus polliciti, particulariter ipsi tentauerunt. E quorum numero primum introduximus exempli causa propositi Caesar rem Augustum, cuius occultum scribendi modum sic manifestum. Spiramina uocis conceptae ex lucidis mutauit in opaca, quorum barbariem uotis renitentem, pulchra quadam adinuentione metatheseos orchemate, conuenientẽ ad nutũ effecit. Hoc est, Magnus Caesar Augustus quo secretè ac tuto scriberet quod uoluit, alphabeti literas uaria transpositione mu- tauit, ita ut poneret B pro A.C.pro B.& sic consequenter de singulis. Et quo scriptura magis tortuosa maneret secretior, pro suo arbitrio lite- ras transposuit in latum et longum ad quamlibet ordinis numeri et loci di- stantiam. Preface to the Explanation of the Whole Work of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of [Paeapolis?], that is, of Würzburg, at St James.

No one who has read these things, I trust, will judge me either proud or superfluous because I myself have provided a commentary on the Polygraphy recently composed by me, especially if he has been able to weigh exactly what cause led us to speak obscurely. For whatever, if made public, can do harm had reasonably to be concealed in mystical language. But the subject which we treat in the Polygraphy is, among good men, very good, useful, and honorable for the advantage of the commonwealth; and for that reason, persuaded by a rational cause, we wrote it down, so that by its service we might render good men safe and secure from the investigation of the wicked when they communicate their secrets to one another. But lest an opportunity be offered to the depraved and perverse, who very frequently misuse even good inventions, to deceive the simpler and less cautious in their judgment of things, we handed down in it mystical or hidden modes of writing, and covered the truth lying hidden in the marrow with certain coverings of figures. Yet we by no means doubt that any industrious man, eager with desire for these matters, will easily grasp everything, if he applies even a moderate persistence in searching them out. For the things I have handed down are not so difficult, nor wrapped in such great mysteries, that they cannot be thoroughly penetrated by a studious man. For everywhere we have so tempered the riddles of our words that they are easily accessible to learned and studious men, and nevertheless remain inaccessible to sluggish men of darkness. But after it pleased us to dedicate and offer the work of the Polygraphy itself to the most serene and most invincible Caesar of the Romans, Maximilian, ever august emperor of the world, I judged it worth the trouble to make it clear and open with brief and few explanations, lest the mind of his sacred majesty, which is daily burdened by many affairs and cares, be drawn back from understanding it by the opacity of the mysteries. For unless my opinion deceives me, the work will be so much the more pleasing and useful to his majesty, the briefer and clearer it has been. Therefore, first of all, with the Lord granting it, we shall briefly explain the meaning of our proposal, which is contained in the prologue wrapped in various riddles; then, through the individual books of the Polygraphy and the modes of operation, the rules, precautions, and distinctions, we shall succinctly set forth, according to order, what necessary things remain, as far as the powers of our intellect allow. All these things, so that they may more quickly become accessible to those who desire to know, we shall show in sequence by examples, and we shall be as brief as the cause and reason permit.

Key to the Explanation of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of [Paeapolis?].

Exposition on the Prologue.

Our whole intention in the entire work of the Polygraphy turns upon this purpose: to hand down certain modes of writing secretly, through which kings and princes, noble and ignoble, priests and laymen, learned and unlearned alike, may secretly, safely, and without any suspicion of a hidden secret, by the service of letters, communicate to one another and to any friends, even those far distant from one another, whatever conception of their minds may be necessary and as often as it may be necessary. And lest we should seem to have presumed to do this either first or alone

[unclear], we forewarn the reader that many of the ancients long ago, especially tyrants, princes, and kings, moved by a similar consideration, devised for themselves familiar and various methods and rules of writing, by which they themselves attempted in particular what we have promised universally in our Polygraphia.

From their number, first, for the sake of an example of the proposed matter, we introduced Caesar Augustus, whose secret method of writing is thus made plain. He changed the breathings of conceived speech from clear letters into obscure ones; and their barbarism, resisting his wishes, by a certain fine invention, by the movement of metathesis, he made obedient to his command. That is: the great Caesar Augustus, in order to write secretly and safely what he wished, changed the letters of the alphabet by various transposition, so that he put B for A, C for B, and so consequently for each one. And so that the writing might remain more twisted and more secret, at his discretion he transposed the letters in breadth and length to any distance of order, number, and place.

Mystery. And this receptive order, as though perpetual, subject to the will and to the reckoning of time, although it keeps messengers safe on the road from the attack of [unclear], nevertheless, since it has no regulated limits, makes all who encounter it anxious with suspicion of a hidden matter.

Explanation. Although no one can easily comprehend with the understanding the secret mystery hidden beneath the transposition of letters, nevertheless this writing makes those into whose hands it comes suspicious about the hiding-place of the matter enclosed within.

Mystery. That Archimedes of Syracuse, easily the foremost of mathematicians, [unclear] his white bird, suitable to his institutions, bare through head and feet, and the rest.

Explanation. Archimedes had two little rods made, of one length and thickness, rounded or squared, of which he kept one with himself and delivered the other to his absent friend. And whenever he wished to write something more secretly to the other, he wrapped the bird, that is, a sheet of papyrus of small width but of the length of the doubled rod, around the wood, and bound it below and above with wax. Afterwards he wrote on the sheet, continuously from the sides, artificially joined together into a mass, whatever he wished; then he released the sheet from the rod, and at once there appeared such a distance between the letters that not even one word cohered with another. and when he wished he wrote in like manner on the other side. Nor was there anyone ignorant of this device who could have discovered the secret. But the man who had the other rod, when he had received the sheet, fastened it on and restored the letters to their earlier order.

Mystery. Marcus T. Cicero, the eloquent orator of the Romans, using both talent and art, changed the minutiae of phrasing into signs, and so forth.

Explanation. He wrote for his son a book of signs, which the blessed martyr Cyprian afterwards enlarged for the use of Christians, namely in the manner of a dictionary, where first the characters or signs are set down in order, and afterwards the words designated by the same characters, so that any given word is signified by the sign placed before it. Written in these signs or characters we once saw an entire Latin psalter, beautifully copied, in the library of the greater church of Strasbourg; some man, ignorant as a judge of things, had placed on its outside the following title: “A Psalter in the Armenian language.” But he was mistaken, since it should rather have been written thus: “A Latin Psalter written in Tullian characters.” For each character represents one Latin word.

Nor does my assessment deceive me, since I possess the very dictionary of Cicero, corrected by Saint Cyprian, written complete and uncorrupted in an old volume, which I have seen nowhere else. So great is the abundance of signs or characters, with the words subject to them, that they are altogether sufficient for writing in the Latin tongue whatever you wish.

Mystery. Faramund, the forty-third from Marcomer, king of the Franks, when in the year of the Lord’s birth 424 he powerfully entered the borders of the Gauls, and so forth.

Explanation. From the time when, in the year 430 before the birth of Christ, the kings of the Franks went forth with their people from the Scythian territories to the mouths of the Rhine, where Guelders now is, they waged continuous war with the Gauls for almost nine hundred years, and at last violently made them subject to themselves, as we have written in the first volume of our Annals. Of these, the aforementioned King Faramund, in order to send messengers safely through the kingdom, devised new letters peculiar to himself, which no one could know without his voluntary instruction. Nor did he use only one, nor a few, but many new alphabets.

of those [unclear], who subjected all Gaul to himself, after the Romans whom he found in it had been destroyed, used his fathers’ inventions for written secrets. Explanation. This king devised alphabets of his own and new ones, and handed one to each of his commanders, and he alone kept with himself knowledge of them all. Mystery. Charles, called the Great, the sixty-third king of the Franks, who first of the Franks wore the diadem of the Roman Empire, and the rest. Explanation. This elder son of King Pippin is read to have been born as duke of Brabant in the county of Namur, bordering on the people of Liège, although some assert that he was born in the village of Ingelheim, not far from Mainz. He also invented various modes of writing, and, with Nanno the grammarian lending his assistance, devised different alphabets, by which he communicated secrets in a special way to the governors of the kingdom. Mystery. The Northmen, having once gone forth from the borders of Gothia, when they were laying waste Gaul with a cruel incursion, called in owls from Greece and prepared a safe hiding-place for their secrets, and the rest. Explanation. The Northmen, roaming through Gaul, as Bede the monk in England bears witness, in order to write their secrets safely among themselves, substituted Greek numerals for Latin letters, from A, the first, up to the twenty-fourth point, such as W, or gu, according to the custom of the Gauls. This mode of writing is altogether very beautiful: in it all the letters are Greek, and according to the Greek order of numbering they designate our Latin letters, as A, 1; B, 2; C, 3; D, 4; E, 5; F, 6; G, 7; and so consequently up to W, which is 24. Neither a Greek nor a Latin will understand this writing, unless he has first learned the method of the device and the art. Mystery. Our Bede, a monk in England, not ignorant of the deed of the Northmen, described many inventions of the ancients similar to these, by which they made what was clear dark in their mysteries. He [unclear], and the rest. Explanation. This Bede, the monk, in his little book on the inventions of the ancients, reviewed many and various modes of writing and noting secretly, by which they safely reported their secrets to friends and spoke without voice to those present. He was the first of all to commit artrology and dactylogy to letters; by the use of these one person most safely discloses to another whatever secret he wishes, which no one else sitting by will notice, much less understand.

He taught that this very thing could be done in many other ways too; since we have written nothing about these in the Polygraphia, we rightly decline to say more about them here. We long ago assigned a proper place for these very difficult matters in the Steganographia, which we do not yet intend to publish publicly. And who could set forth all the modes of secret writing among the ancients? For some had as familiars in the service of the proposed art owls called Philophotos, others Mysophotos, others called both into practice from the art. Again, some transposed the known letters of the common alphabet; others devised their own characters for themselves under the form of those of barbarians. Again also, some used the service of visible letters, writing with minium or ordinary encaustic; others, however, formed invisible characters at their own will on command. The modes of visible characters for secret writing are very many and utterly innumerable; to mention all of them belongs neither to our will nor to our power. Of invisible characters, however, there are three kinds more commonly used among mortals today. The first is called dermatic, by which a certain artificial writing is made on the backs of messengers, visible only through the washing of a certain fluid [unclear]. The [second?] is written in cloth with a certain penetrating [unclear], which, when dried, can by no means be seen until, when moistened in cold water, it is perceived. The third kind is named alleotic, which is manifold and various, both in form and in material, and has almost innumerable modes of writing secretly. Its writing is done on paper or without paper, with [nemilua] and [cala], with [raphocam], [lapolce], and other diverse things. Letters are likewise written in various ways and hidden in places, as under [race tabulata], under [rosi rilacubior], in [leopi], in [necostas], in [ceocali], [locubat], in [ratera], in [lispilia], and in other similar things almost infinite in number. But because none of these things on this occasion serves our purpose, therefore it is fitting that we hasten to those matters which the plan demands. There is also another kind, dactiletron, not of writing, however, but of signs, by which one person can make known the conception of his mind to another in very subtle ways. This too is varied by so many differences that there is no one in the world who could enumerate all the kinds of so great a mystery. In the principal mode, at the same time

... and many others descending from it artificially, while sitting at table, or in any other place, you will be able to convey whatever you wish, safely, most securely, and without anyone’s suspicion, to one who knows the art. Finally, how, without letters, you may disclose the secret of your mind to someone absent, even without the knowledge of the very person who performs the office of messenger, remains ascribed to the inventions of steganography. For indeed, since kings and princes encounter many affairs about which, at times, they do not trust that knowledge can be given safely enough by customary letters to their deputies far away, it will be worth the effort for each of them to have certain special methods of writing and sending messages, by which they may most securely make their secrets known to friends, especially in these times, in which, with license to sin prevailing, trustworthy faith is found nowhere in the world. Everywhere the messengers of princes are seized by savage robbers, stripped, and very often killed; nor do the impious plunderers spare even the letters of kings sealed and closed with rings. Hence it would be necessary for your commonwealth, O most glorious Emperor Maximilian, that you put on the skin of Hercules, brandish the club in your hands, and purge for yourself, by God’s help, the world entrusted to you of these savage monsters. There will never be peace in the kingdom unless the [unclear] are removed from its midst. He who disturbs the peace of the kingdom shows himself to be the king’s enemy. These are the robbers who beset the roads of travelers, seize others’ goods; with them the earth today is full, and nowhere is the road safe for those walking.

A Brief Explanation of Those Things Which Seem More Obscure in the First Book of the Polygraphia

Although nothing obscure is contained in the first book of the Polygraphia, nevertheless, lest its composition should perhaps seem profound to the simpler sort, we briefly explain those things that are thought more difficult. We have distributed the words of the Latin language, in order, nine thousand in number, under nearly four hundred alphabets, arranged in such sequence that if from any alphabet one word only is taken after another, from the beginning to the end, they will cohere with one another and produce a fitting Latin discourse. For it will be a very suitable method of writing most secretly whatever we wish, since each word represents the letter set before it at its head. And let it not trouble you, reader, that a multitude of words in the open text contains a brief sense in the hidden one, since in this childish arrangement of ours there lies concealed a higher method of writing whatever you wish, more broadly and much more secretly, which public reason has forbidden us to make open to all. But whoever has been endowed with intelligence and has applied the necessary powers to the investigation of the doctrines hidden in these things will discover subtler matters, and things marvelously unknown before; plainly he will understand more marvelous things. Nevertheless, this open method of writing will suffice for all purposes, since you can repeat it as often as you wish, and the repeated narration will always be varied. For if, as we have said, you take one word from the first alphabet, likewise one from the second, and so consequently one from each, and one from those placed between, outside the ordered line, up to the period or the end of the book, a Latin and sufficiently fitting discourse will arise for you. But care must be taken that at one time, together and once for all, no more than one word be taken from one alphabet, and that the writer, through negligence or excessive haste, not skip over any alphabet and confuse the order of the narration. By “day” understand the open narration; by “night,” however, the hidden and secret one, which should not be too long but brief. The examples that follow in the text, concerning the invisible soul and the body that is seen, pertain to both narrations, the hidden and the manifest. “Whenever a leaf is moved by the wind,” and the rest: we advise that you count the secret narration in relation to the open one in such a way that both at once end at the foot of each period. But if anything remains over from the secret matter, let it be enlarged with such moderation that both narrations end at one point, lest a confusion of eclipse be produced. The other things that follow in the first Polygraphic book are implicitly referred to the document of explanation and to all the things that we have said. It should be noted, however, that under the order of the alphabets there is no idle word, but each one represents the letter set before it at its head; and lest the reader lack perfect knowledge of this matter, let us explain by an example. Let us suppose the case that a wicked man seeks through you to be promoted with some friend of yours, but you, wishing to cut off his troublesome requests and yet not promote an unworthy man...

... you may [unclear], thus to write more secretly to a friend through the very man who asks for it, so that he may not understand. “Beware of that man, because he is a thief and the worst scoundrel.” Go to the first alphabet: write the word “Creator,” which signifies C; in the second, “merciful,” which gives A; in the third, “discerning,” which represents V; in the fourth, “worldly things,” and it signifies E. Now you have, in the hidden narration, “beware.” Proceed in sequence also through the other alphabets, and the discourse will come out as follows: “May the merciful Creator, discerning worldly things, impart to those who seek it seraphic delight with all his saints in heaven, amen. The gentleness of the most glorious prince, everywhere reverently to be remembered by the saints, urges us, most abject sleepers, by the best precepts, to forsake present things because of reverence for the director of good things, and with every affection, according to our powers, to await the glory of perpetual rest. Therefore, O vain mockers, receive instruction, so that you may be able, most happily adorned, to enter the most blessed rejoicings of the [unclear] rewarder of the orthodox. Rise therefore from the foulest honors of this pilgrimage, since you are about to enter most holily into the most blessed joys of the kindly Savior of the ages.” In this public narration set down above there is contained in secret this hidden sentence, namely: “Beware of that man, because he is a thief and the worst scoundrel, but be silent, I pray.” The same order must be followed in all other cases whatsoever; one must begin from the head as often as necessary, until you have enclosed the hidden narration of your secret clearly. But the words that are placed outside the order of the alphabet, since they designate no letter and do not serve the hidden narration, have been inserted because of a lack of synonyms, so that the sequence of Latin discourse might be completed. For we could not always have so many words with the same meaning, especially among pronouns, conjunctions, prepositions, and interjections, that we could have made an alphabet in place of twenty-four wandering letters, as is clearly evident after the eighth alphabet, where we placed two words outside the order, lest we leave the discourse defective. For thus we placed them, and thus: “with all.” Of these the writer may choose two, so that the Latin discourse may be completed. Let him do likewise in the others, whenever he finds similar cases. We have adopted a double M because of our native speech, in which we frequently need it in our German language. For one who is ignorant of Latin speech may write his hidden secret in German beneath a Latin discourse without any difficulty.

Now follow the rules or cautions to be observed in the operation of this book.

The first rule or caution warns you that the secret of your mind which you wish to announce to an absent friend, one who knows the art and has the book of Polygraphy, you should write on a sheet as carefully as you can, in Latin or German, or in any other language you wish that can be comprehended by Roman letters. Then place the sheet so written before you, so that for each single letter of the secret you can fit an appropriate word. For, as we have shown in this practice of writing, a whole word is taken. We gave an example a little earlier in what was set down above.

II. The second caution instructs you, as has been said, not to take more than one word at the same time from any alphabet in a single narration of public Latin discourse; otherwise you would both confuse the open sense and entirely draw away from understanding the secret the friend to whom you had written.

III. Third, one must take the utmost care not to skip through negligence any alphabet from which you do not take one word appropriate to the secret. Likewise provision must be made that, whenever one or more words occur outside the series of the alphabet, you take the whole upper line or the lower one, and not both.

IIII. Fourth, care must be taken that whenever the discourse of the open speech has been brought to a completed sentence, the following sentence should take its beginning from a larger, thickened letter, according to the form of the preceding example, in which, according to the sense of the Latin discourse, we have taken capital letters at the beginning and small ones in the rest, in the common manner. When the secret of your mind is lengthy, so that it exceeds the narration of the open discourse, if much remains, you should begin again from the beginning; if little remains, let the discourse be brought back at will from whatever place one likes. For no one even moderately skilled in this practice will be unable to know where you have begun again. Nor is it necessary to fear the consonan[unclear].

EXPLANATIO LIBRI Polygraphiae nostrae quarti. IN quarto Polygraphiae libro simili ratione dictiones à nobis confictas sub ordine alphabetico locauimus, sed in uno solo consultè à praecedente discrepamus. Nam in praecedente libro nihil in se dictiones proprietatis aliud continent, nisi quod literas à capite sibi praepositas repraesenting. In quarto autem libro quem nunc uersamus in manibus singulae dictiones proprium uitorem continent, & litteras nihilominus antepositas designant, Intus habent quod foris exhibent, quia secunda litera cuiusque distionis occulto semper deseruit mysterio, q̃ sequenti manifestum faciemus exēplo. Ecorach hanasar dulay semalas, choriō suriel anephor schabaras husarat uiimalo tropon tumelech amasar. Pro huius intellectu mysterij dequalibet qualibet dictione secundā duntaxat litera accipito et inuenies hūc sensum latentè, Caue hunc uirũ. Nã secunda litera in Ecorach est C, in hanafar= A, in dulay V, in semalas E, coniunge has quatuor literas et facient hoc urbum, Caue Sicque procedatur in reliquis usque ad finem libri, et si quid oc culti restat mysterij scribendum, totiens recurratur ad principium, donec arcanũ in toto fuerit completũ. In hoc modo secretißimè scribendi, si quis per longũ usum fuerit exercitus libro non indiget, sed ex tempore dictio nes suo proposito convenientes facile componet. Qui aūt minus in compo mendo exercitus fuerit, libri copiam de quo scribat necessario requirit. Lectori exemplar vuminis non erit necessariũ quippe cũ sine libro per litteras ubique secundas facile latens queat inuenire secretum. In rebus tamẽ magnis, arduis aut periculosis, huic modo scribendi non satis tuto credere cur, propter ea q̃ industria periti hõis à casu posset occultũ inuenire myste rium. Potest autē et iste modus scribendi per uirum intelligentem mutari, ut litterae significantes in tertio uel in quarto dictionis loco ponantur distionibus alteratis. let him who receives letters written from the Polygraphia to be read know that understanding is needed in the reading. And therefore, whenever he takes up a sheet or booklet written polygraphically, let him go to a secret place; and, having opened the book of the Polygraphia, which he ought to have with him, let him consider each word through all the alphabets, and let him most carefully note with chalk on the table, or with ink on paper, what letter each one represents. And when he has examined the whole letter in that way, let him put the letters together into words, and he will easily understand what has lain hidden in secrecy. XII. Twelfth, kings and princes should note this, who have many vicars in different places, to all of whom it is not prudent to write by one kind of hidden narration. Therefore, so that they may have their own secret manner of writing to each one individually, let them change the order of the words as many times as they wish to have separate methods. Thus they themselves will possess the writing methods of all, and none of their subjects will understand another’s method. For the variable methods of writing more secretly in this art are infinite. XIII. Thirteenth, it must be noted that, in order to stop the mouths of those who speak wicked things, we show the truth of this new invention of ours to be possible, placing the words in the alphabets of the first book so coherently with one another that, in the manner of an exhortation and supplication offered to God, they render a fitting and Latin prayer. Beneath its narration we can conceal the secrets that occur to us and write in such a way to a friend skilled in the art that, if all the people in the whole world were to come together into one place, they could never discover the secret lying hidden beneath the open discourse, provided it has been arranged correctly. XIIII. Fourteenth, it should be known that in this very invention of our Polygraphia there still lie hidden certain things far better than those described above, namely how you will be able, in a few days, not to say hours, to instruct someone ignorant of the Latin language so that he knows how to write, read, and understand Latin: not, indeed, absolutely everything universally, but, according to a certain method, whatever necessary thing comes before him in his affairs on any subject. Likewise, in what manner you may make known safely, securely, and most secretly to your friend far absent, and knowing the practice of the art, all the conceptions of your mind, without writings and without the messenger knowing; indeed sometimes without a messenger, naturally and without

Some superstition, danger, or fear. But reason has moved us to let these things remain buried in their hiding-places with the rest, since it neither pleases me nor is at all expedient to throw away precious stones once found, and to undertake difficult things without the fruit of gratitude. In short, beneath these things there lie no small subtle mysteries concerning medicines, herbs, plants, precious stones, rivers, the members of the human body, brute animals, saints, nations, cosmography and the seven liberal arts, and also concerning all those things that are in human use, and concerning the whole world, both of visible and invisible things. And, lest we be more prolix than is proper, all things that are in the world, through the expansion of the likeness shown beforehand, serve the mystical teaching of the art of polygraphy.

XV. Fifteenth, note that all these things which we have handed down as discoveries in the Polygraphy are certain small introductions in comparison with those which still remain to be discovered and written in this same faculty; concerning these we pass over in silence, lest we should seem to boast in vain. For we have given suitable minds the occasion for discovering greater things than we either have written or perhaps could have discovered. Let him who can add, for the completion of this aid, those things which he knows to be useful; but let him who cannot, not rashly judge what he does not understand.

Explanation of Those Things Which Seemed More Obscure in the Second Book of the Polygraphy.

In the second book of the Polygraphy, apart from the order and sequence of the words, [unclear]; and therefore there will be one and the same method of operating in both, and we carefully warn that all the things which we said must be observed in the first are also to be observed in the second. The difference is seen to have arisen plainly in the narration alone, since the former is composed concerning our Lord, the Son of God, but this one is raised up to his mother, the ever-untouched Virgin. Now in the second book there are three hundred and eight alphabets set in order before the words, though under different subjects. For from the beginning the narration of the discourse is directed to that same Lady of ours; afterwards the Lord’s Prayer is expanded under twenty-four alphabets; then [unclear]

Abrin madon badis, cadulur pasu, adin loroff masara damis, boda omo dro mi drus uares mastron pha lares medas rassut madebor tara, mesen baiu phosat, galos, prosol fane lemoros, arosocabil neso, hamol heliet rhamil fesia doron hubor rodex.

In this narration of fictive speech there is contained this brief secret sentence, of a friend warning a friend about danger: Do not come to the court, because the king is angry with you. You see how easy, safe, and secure this method becomes for writing and announcing whatever you wish to the friend who understands it. Yet in all things you should know that care must be taken, as was said before, that you do not take more than one word from any alphabet. Whenever you have carried the narration of the contrived discourse to the end of the book, while the secret of your mind is not yet complete, begin again from the beginning, and do this as often as shall be necessary. Nevertheless, each person may, at his own judgment, change these words of ours, improve them, and add more, provided however that he avoid a consonance that breaks out shamefully in the sounds.

Explanation of the Fourth Book of Our Polygraphy.

In the fourth book of the Polygraphy, by a similar method, we have placed the words contrived by us in alphabetical order, but in one respect alone we deliberately differ from the preceding book. For in the preceding book the words contain in themselves nothing else of property except that they represent the letters set before them at the head. But in the fourth book, which we now have in hand, each word contains its own [unclear], and nevertheless designates the letters placed before it. They have within what they display without, because the second letter of each word always serves the hidden mystery, as we shall make clear by the following example. In any word take only the second letter, and you will find this sense hidden: “Beware this man.” For the second letter in Ecorach is C, in hanafar A, in dulay V, in semalas E. Join these four letters and they will make this word: Cave. And so one proceeds through the rest to the end of the book; and if anything remains to be written of the hidden mystery, one must return to the beginning as often as necessary, until the secret has been wholly completed. In this most secret manner of writing, if anyone has been trained by long practice, he has no need of a book, but will easily compose on the spot words suited to his purpose. But he who has had less practice in composing necessarily requires a copy of the book from which he may write.

For the reader, a copy of the volume will not be necessary, since without the book he can easily find the hidden secret by means of the second letters everywhere. Yet in great, difficult, or dangerous matters, this manner of writing is not considered sufficiently safe, because by the ingenuity of a skilled man the hidden mystery might by chance be discovered. This manner of writing can also be altered by an intelligent man, so that the significant letters are placed in the third or fourth position of the word, with the words changed.

Brief explanation of the fifth book of our Polygraphia.

[unclear]

In the fifth book of the Polygraphia we have handed down various ways of writing secretly by transposition of the common letters, arranged in such an order that under their covering we shall be able to write and report everything safely to an absent friend. Now, to speak in our own manner, the progression of the transposition of letters is almost infinite, since from one alphabet by metathesis innumerable alphabets arise. First we described a straight table containing twenty-four alphabets; through understanding it, as many alphabets can be composed as there are stars counted in the firmament of heaven. For as many letters as there are in that table, so many times there arise by the art, in order, one million alphabets. After this we set out a reversed table, which will arise into another as often as you change the first letter at the head.

The letter in the first straight table is B, and in the reversed table Z. Into the fourth place [unclear]

All the synthemata of this book are sufficiently clear and manifest, and therefore they need no explanation, not even a brief one. Yet those things which have been newly invented by us require a definite declaration, lest perhaps they be judged to have been set down without reason. First of all, we made all the letters of the Latins numerical, after the manner of the Hebrews and Greeks, considering it shameful for us if we should be found inferior to them in this respect. For what if we have doubled certain letters so that they might suffice for an infinite number, since the Jews, compelled by the same necessity, did the very same thing long ago? And the Greeks, because of the lack of letters, admitted certain signs into the number, since they were unable to double the letters. But we, because we are pressed by an equal lack of letters, admit two signs: namely this &, which our writers put for et; nor does it matter whether it is written thus, &, or thus, et, provided it represents six in the number. We have added another, 9, which our writers, when abbreviating, write indifferently for con and com; and here in the order of numbers it represents six hundred. By the same necessity we have doubled two letters, namely r, z, and s: of these r means ninety, but curved z means one hundred, long s two hundred, and closed s three hundred. Further, doubled w, which because of the character of the German language we have placed in the order of the alphabet, represents the last letter, and in the series of numbers one thousand. Let us set down a tabular example of this new invention of ours for the reckoning of numbers, so that anyone who wishes to know the method may have a definite demonstration before his eyes. For what has always been easy for the Hebrews and Greeks will not be impossible for us. The table of numbers follows.

We have shown a sufficient method of counting by Latin letters in the manner of the Hebrews and Greeks, which by way of digression we have reasonably placed here, although it is found earlier in the sixth book. By the fact that, as we proceeded, we have here concluded our number at thirty hundred thousands, we plainly declare that it can be extended to infinity. If this method of numbers displeases anyone, he will easily be able to devise a better one. In imitation also of the Northmen, from the numerical letters set out above, we have arranged a new alphabet, by which you will be able safely to write and report to an absent friend any secret whatsoever you wish. Indeed this method of writing is as secret as it is new, never seen or heard before us, so that it seems to me altogether impossible that it can be understood by anyone without the service of a teacher. But now let us set down its alphabet.

Behold, you now have here an alphabet from numerical letters in imitation of the Northmen, with which you will be able to write and report most safely to an absent friend whatever you wish. No one lying hidden will be able to penetrate the secret except him who knows the secret of the art. For all who see the writing will think that the letters have been transposed, and they will labor in vain in reckoning them. Let us set down an example: Iaaihidifeib, iceigeicchkib. cal'eihid.iei [unclear]ahk.gidibidi[unclear]ig. eiif.iaaihifidibe icda a.cih.iceieik. The hidden meaning of this writing is as follows: Beware the bearer of the present letters, because he is a very wicked man, a thief, a robber, a liar, worthless. From the demonstration of this example it is easily given to be understood how safe and secure this method of writing is universally, in every language known to the writer, and in every cause or business, however difficult, secret, great, or lengthy. Nor do I think there is a man living in the world who by his own ingenuity, without a teacher, can read this very writing. For all who see it will think nothing other than that the letters have been transposed; and when they cannot obtain an understanding of them, at last worn out by despair they will cease from the investigation, and whatever you have written will remain hidden. For no one, as I suppose, will examine by his own powers this craft of writing secretly as it is, unless he has Polygraphy, or this key to it, at hand, or has been instructed by another. From these numerical letters many other alphabets can also be given according to the order of counting, when the beginning for writing alphabetically is taken not from unity but from any other following number. But in that progression you should know that one must beware lest more than two countable letters be taken to represent one letter. Therefore, when you have come to vovo, that is, ten hundred thousands, stop your advance and do not wander farther, lest the multitude of letters, by spoiling the beauty of writing, confound it. For, after unity has been set aside, ten hundred thousand, with [unclear] letters included, suffice for nearly thirty separate alphabets. Nevertheless the method of the first alphabet, beginning with unity, is so much the fairer for wrapping secrets in writing as it is shorter and simpler. Finally, it renders the writing less contorted.

We have also arranged another alphabet, with the Latin letters distributed in a continuous order and transposed without a rule, in imitation of which others too can be made almost without number; and its likeness is now set down.

rie, de Romani Imperij Principis Electoris, Philosophorum Sapientissimi Mecaenatis, quo nullus dignior mihi uisus est, cui hoc magnum secretum re ueletur literis commendaui, & in subiectum volumen, non sine ingenti la- bore reduxi, ne hoc magnum Secretum, in aures vulgarium imperatorum, aut prauorum hominum perueniat. Te Lector quicunque futurus es, rogo me mineris, quanta per hanc scientiam mala in Republica fieri per malos et lubricos possent, si ad multorum notitiam deueniret, adulteria, fornica tiones, conspirationes, traditiones, homicidia, latrocinia et infinita mala. Nam sicut bonus et honestus homo voluntatis suae secreturn alteri hanc ar tem scienti, quotie scunque uoluerit pro utilitate priuata uel communi, se- cure, & absque aliqua suspitione cuiuscunque notificare potest et exprime re: & peruersus quisque, lubricus, & maliciosus, uoluptatis suae personae consentanea quantumlibet, turpiter impedimento penitus omni semoto, malum desiderium suum, sine aliqua suspitione poterit intimare. Nec tuta inter coniugatos fides manere iam deinceps posset, dum femina, quamuis latini sermonis haec tenus inscia, per sancta et pudica uerba cuiuslibet lin- guae seu ideomatis effecta doctissima, malam et impudicam amatoris sui seu uoluntatem, uiro licet preferente ac collaudante literas, latissime intelligere, supque desiderium eodem modo securissime quam uoluerit. Late illi remandare, diserta satis oratione possit. Enimuero, licet haec sci entia puerilis uideri aliquibus poßit, tamen si fuerit publicata totus Rei publicae ordo turbaretur, fides periret publica, litterae, instrumenta scriptu rae, omnes ipsi denique hominum sermones, in perpetuam suspicionem uer- terentur. Nemo iam literis quantumcunque bonis, honestis et sanctis am plius crederet, fidem epistolis nullus adhiberet, quoniam, quantumlibet sancta et pudica uerba fuerint, semper tamen dolus fraus et mala dece- ptio subesse putaretur, fierentque homines ad omnia timidi, et non minus ad mutuos sermones, quoniam ad literas quasi libet suspiciosi. Nec fieri quis- piam tam doctus et expertus in hac ipsa scientia unquam poterit, ut non relinquantur infiniti modi, secretè et occultissimè scribendi ad omnia sufficientes, quos ipse nondum apprehendit. Est enim haec scientia chao chaos infinitae magnitudinis, quod nemo cõpraehẽdere potest. Quia quam tumlibet doctus in hac arte fueris, minus tamen est quod intelligis, quam illud quod nescis. Nam huius scientiae proprietas est, Magis stro discipulum semper, modo fit industrius et uelit, redde re sine comparatione doctiorem. Let us also set down an example of this alphabet, to prove that a secret can be hidden in it. Gquog, o[unclear]uqi, yar, din, u, c, qacquxua, riqdi u[unclear]i, aqqurixr 12, siti, idta, yocsaqui g, uc, coddotacuo[unclear], osoqui, iug, g, cj, hidiog. This writing contains in itself the following meaning: Know, friend, that the king in council has decreed that you are to be killed. Therefore flee as quickly as possible into Narragonia from his presence, lest you perish. This manner of writing too is tortuous, and is subject to no regular norm, since it can be varied and changed by arbitrary transposition at the writer's pleasure as much as anyone wishes. Next, it should be noted that we have handed down numerals, which people commonly call ciphers, under whose covering you will safely write to an absent friend whatever you wish, and no one unskilled in the art will be able either to discover or suspect that a secret lies hidden, especially if the rules that we have given concerning these things are observed with careful diligence. This is that the paper should be formed in the manner of an astronomical table, as though it contained something pertaining to the reckoning of the stars, namely so that the characters of the signs or planets are interspersed, in order that someone into whose hands it perhaps happens to fall, led by its tabular appearance, may think that no secret lies hidden in it, but may suppose that everything pertains to some astronomical calculation. We have arranged twelve alphabets according to the number of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, assigning to each a number of twenty-four in place of the letters; the first of these, Aries, begins from one and ends at twenty-four. Yet in great and difficult matters we advise beginning from one, because that manner of writing can easily be suspect for that very reason. But whoever wishes prudently to use natural industry will find subtler things from ours, and will easily make better the things that we have handed down not sufficiently polished. In the numerical orchema great secrets lie hidden; if anyone understands them properly, he will penetrate many mysteries of numbers. For we had neither the time nor the reason on this occasion to pour everything out into public view; but in our judgment what we have done will suffice for the instruction of those to whom they will someday be pleasing, so that they may have several methods not only of writing secretly whatever they wish to absent sharers in the undertaking, but also a way of bringing forth one method into several better and subtler ones according to the capacity of each person's understanding. Likewise, since the numerical orchemata are sufficiently open and manifest in their own places, and their tables likewise set out, it was not necessary here to repeat what has once been said, lest excessive length produce weariness for the reader. Nor did I think it necessary to set down an example of more secret writing by means of the figures of numbers, since there is no difficulty in knowing the method for all who are strong in even a moderate intelligence. With similar ease the very useful signs of numbering that we have brought back to light can be understood and comprehended, by which knowledge of numbers is extended to infinity. For whenever a small stroke is placed above a lesser number, a thousand is signified. Thus xͣ signifies ten thousand, C one hundred thousand, M a thousand thousand, X ten times a thousand thousand; .M. signifies a thousand times a thousand thousand, and so in succession, as far as you wish to proceed in numbering, without limit.

Apology of Johannes Trithemius Prefixed to the Steganographia

It is the opinion of many that the ancient philosophers and wise men of art and nature, if they had discovered any secrets, concealed them in various ways and figures, lest they should come to the knowledge of wicked men. That Moses also, the most famous leader of the Israelite people, in his description of the creation of heaven and earth, covered ineffable secrets of mysteries with simple words, all the more learned among the Jews confirm. Saint Jerome too, most learned among our own, says that almost as many mysteries lie hidden in the Apocalypse as there are words. Moreover the wise men of the Greeks, men of no small reputation and glory among their people, who devoted their efforts to composing fables, handed down one thing to the unlearned and another to learned men, in the course of a single narrative, by a prudent invention.

These most zealous lovers of wisdom, even if because of the slowness of my intellect I cannot imitate them perfectly, nevertheless I judge it fine and glorious to admire, and with such diligence as I can to read and venerate. Thus, when I consider that they, by their own study, discovered great things beyond other men, I drive myself, doing a kind of violence to myself, toward some imitation of them, even if among the very last. Nor, as I think, has my opinion altogether deceived me; for through continual zeal in reading I have learned many things which I had not known before, and I have opened [the way] to my thoughts for investigating more secret matters.

For even if I am not of such learning or industry that I dare profess that I have comprehended that method of the ancient wise men for concealing mysteries, nevertheless I have devised certain methods, not altogether contemptible, as it seems to me, of writing and concealing secretly, and wholly without any suspicion, whatever you wish. At the request of the most serene prince, lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, prince-elector of the Roman Empire, the wisest Maecenas of philosophers, than whom no one seemed to me more worthy to whom this great secret should be revealed, I committed them to writing and reduced them into the following volume, not without immense labor, lest this great Secret come to the ears of common emperors or wicked men.

Reader, whoever you will be, I ask you to consider how many evils could be done in the commonwealth by evil and wanton men through this science if it came to the knowledge of many: adulteries, fornications, conspiracies, betrayals, murders, robberies, and infinite evils. For just as a good and honorable man can safely and without any suspicion from anyone make known and express the secret of his will, as often as he wishes, for private or common advantage, to another who knows this art, so every perverse, wanton, and malicious man will be able to intimate his evil desire, however shamefully, to a person agreeable to his pleasure, with every obstacle entirely removed and without any suspicion.

Nor could trust between married persons thereafter remain secure, since a woman, although up to this point ignorant of the Latin tongue, made most learned through holy and modest words of any language or idiom, could understand very fully the evil and shameless will of her lover, even while her husband presents and praises the letters; and in the same way she could most safely send back to him her own desire, as widely as she wished, in sufficiently eloquent speech. Indeed, although this science may seem childish to some, nevertheless if it were made public the whole order of the commonwealth would be disturbed, public trust would perish, letters, written instruments, and finally all the very speech of men would be turned into perpetual suspicion. No one would any longer trust letters, however good, honorable, and holy; no one would put faith in epistles, since, however holy and modest the words might be, nevertheless deceit, fraud, and evil deception would always be thought to lie beneath, and men would become fearful in all things, and no less suspicious toward mutual conversations than toward any letters at all.

Nor will anyone ever be able to become so learned and experienced in this very science that there will not remain infinite methods of writing secretly and most hiddenly, sufficient for all things, which he himself has not yet grasped. For this science is a chao

a chaos of infinite magnitude, which no one can comprehend. For however learned you may have been in this art, what you understand is still less than what you do not know. For it is the property of this science always to make the pupil, provided he is industrious and willing, incomparably more learned than the teacher.

There follows the exposition of the very distinguished man Adolf Glauburg, patrician of Frankfurt, with examples of matters which were either passed over by the author or treated less clearly.

Magnus, from these, emperor of the Romans. On this method of writing, see Suetonius Tranquillus in the Life of Augustus, chapter 83, and in the Life of Julius Caesar, chapter 80. “There are extant,” he says, “letters to Cicero, and likewise to his friends, concerning domestic matters, in which, if anything had to be conveyed rather secretly, he wrote it by signs, that is, with the order of the letters so arranged that no word could be formed; if anyone wished to investigate these, he should substitute the fourth letter of the alphabet, that is, d, for a, and change the rest in the same way.” Moreover Isidore also mentions a letter of Augustus to his son, in which he writes thus: “Since countless things continually occur which one or the other of us ought to write, and which ought to be secret, let us have signs between ourselves, if you wish, of such a kind that when something has to be written by us, for each single letter we write the following one, in this way: b for a, c for b, and thereafter the others by the same method. But for the letter z one must return to double aa.”

Archimedes of Syracuse. Similar to this is what is read in Gellius, book 17, chapter 9. The ancient Lacedaemonians, when they wished to disguise and conceal letters sent publicly to their commanders, so that, if they were intercepted by enemies, their plans would not become known, used to send letters made in this manner. There were two rods, round, somewhat oblong, of equal thickness and the same length, shaved down and finished in like fashion. One was given to the commander setting out for war; the other the magistrates kept at home, under oath and seal. When there was need of more secret letters, around the rod they wrapped a long strap of moderate thinness, or as much as was sufficient for the matter, in a round and single winding, so that the adjoining edges everywhere of the strap that was being folded came together and held fast. Then they wrote the letters on that strap across the joined edges, in lines proceeding from top to bottom. That strap, thus written all over with letters, when unwound from the rod, they sent to the commander, who knew the device. The unwinding of the strap likewise rendered the letters broken and mutilated, and their parts and strokes were scattered into very different places. Therefore, if that strap fell into the hands of enemies, they could infer absolutely nothing from it. But when the man to whom it had been sent received it, taking the matching rod which he had, he wrapped it around it to the end, just as he knew it had to be done; and thus the letters, coming together along the same circumference of the rod, joined again and provided a complete and uncorrupted letter, easy to read. The Lacedaemonians call this kind of letter a scytale. See also Plutarch in the Life of Lysander.

There is also another, no less ingenious, method of concealing letters, described by Jerome Cardano in his books On Subtleties. You take two equal sheets of parchment ruled for writing, and in the lines themselves you make small holes scattered here and there opposite one another in both, but nevertheless according to the size or height of the letters. Some will contain seven letters, some three, some eight or ten, so that all the holes together contain one hundred and twenty letters, when all those which can be written in them are joined together. But when there is need, write your first sentence as briefly as you can, so that the number of letters

that the sentence should contain a smaller [number of words?] than that which the spaces admit. Then, on a parchment placed beneath the openings, you will write that sentence, and likewise on another and another; finally fill the spaces of the first parchment, completing and deleting sentences until the sense holds together. You will complete this second sentence on the second parchment in such a way that the words and sentences seem to cohere; on the third also you will fit it so that, without injury to the first letters, the whole sentence, the number and size of the words, agree and retain a certain elegance. When this has been done, place over a parchment of equal size the pattern that you cut out, and at the edges of the openings mark the very finest points, as far as the letters extend which you wish to write. Then take a third parchment, and [write] the letter in continuous words, with a suitable order of spaces and also with suitable size of letters, so that the first sentence and its words are contained within the limits of the points. Therefore no suspicion of deception then remains; when the other man receives it, with the pattern laid over it, he at once understands the thought of your mind. And for this purpose, although it is no light labor, nothing comparable can be found for indicating one’s thought to friends in dangerous times.

Marcus Tullius. The account is that Cicero devised individual and special characters for each Latin word, by which, if necessity demanded, he wrote a speech however long both with very few signs and most secretly. And in this way, they say, Cato’s speech, that the conspirators should be punished, was preserved and committed to writing, when Cicero as consul appointed very swift writers who would take down what was said in notes of this kind. That the ancients also, in writing out words quickly and briefly, followed a somewhat similar method, so that frequently a single letter signified a word, is attested by Valerius Probus, Petrus Crinitus, Angelus Decembrius, and likewise by the very ancient monuments most diligently collected by Petrus Appianus and Bartholomaeus Amantius. But this craft of writing will be treated more diligently hereafter.

Our Bede in England. On computation and the speech of the fingers. These things I find in Bede’s De temporum ratione. When you say one, bending the little finger on the left hand, you will set its joint in the middle of the palm. When you say two, you will place there the second finger from the little finger, bent. When you say three, you will similarly bend the third. When you say four, likewise you will raise the little finger. When you say five, you will similarly raise the second from the little finger. When you say six, you will nevertheless raise the third, with only the finger called the medicus fixed in the middle of the palm. When you say seven, you will place the little finger alone, the rest raised, upon the base of the palm. Next to this, when you say eight, you will set the medicus. When you say nine, you will set the impudicus opposite it. When you say ten, you will set the nail of the index finger in the middle joint of the thumb. When you say twenty, you will put the tip of the thumb between the middle joints of the index finger and the impudicus. When you say thirty, you will join the nails of the index finger and thumb in a gentle embrace. When you say forty, you will draw the inner parts of the thumb over the side or back of the index finger, with only those two raised. When you say fifty, you will bend the thumb at the outer joint, in the manner of the Greek letter called gamma, and incline it toward the palm. When you say sixty, you will carefully gird from the front the thumb, bent as above, with the index finger curved round it. When you say seventy, you will fill the index finger, curved round as above, with the thumb stretched lengthwise, with only its nail raised across the middle joint of the index finger. When you say eighty, you will make the index finger, curved round as above, with the thumb held lengthwise, on the left hand: two hundred on the right, just as [unclear] ten on the left [unclear]. But one hundred on the right, just as [unclear] on the left. Likewise one thousand on the right, just as one on the left. Two thousand on the right, just as two on the left. Three thousand on the right, with only the fingers raised toward the neck. When you say twenty thousand, you will lay the same [hand], spread broadly, over the breast. When you say thirty thousand, with the same [hand] prone but upright, you will put the thumb into the cartilage of the middle of the breast. When you say fifty thousand, the thumb of the same [hand], prone but upright,

[unclear] you will place upon the navel. When you say sixty thousand, with the same [hand] you will grasp the left thigh from above. When you say seventy thousand, you will place the same upon the thigh. When you say eighty thousand, you will place the same [unclear] upon the thigh. When you say ninety thousand, with the same [hand] you will grasp the loins, with the thumb turned toward the groin. But one hundred and two hundred thousand, up to nine hundred thousand, you will complete in the same order that we have described, on the right side of the body. And when you say ten times one hundred thousand, you will clasp both hands together with the fingers [interlaced?]. And so much concerning numbers to be expressed by the gesture of the fingers.

To these the same author immediately adds: "From the very computation which I have noted above, a certain manual speech can also be practiced, both for the sake of exercising ingenuity and of playing a game. By it, when the letters are expressed one by one, a person may convey to another, who also knows this technique, even if he is placed far away, the words contained in those letters, so that they may be read and understood; or he may signify necessary matters more secretly by intimating them in this way, or deceive the unskilled as though by divination. The order of this game or speech is as follows. When you wish to indicate the first letter of the alphabet, hold one with the hand; when the second, two; when the third, three; and so the rest in order. For example, if you wish to warn a friend placed among ambushers to act cautiously, show three and one, and twenty, and ten and nine, and five fingers; for the letters of this order signify 'act cautiously.'"

Thus far the example of dactylogy according to Bede, which is also varied in many other ways. For, once it has been posited, as was also said before, that the sign of unity signifies the letter a, and so on in order, let them be arranged on the left hand: one in the thumb, two in the index finger, three in the middle finger, four in the ring finger, or the third from the thumb, and five in the little finger. Likewise on the right hand let two be understood in the thumb, three in the index finger, four in the middle finger, five in the third from the thumb, and six in the little finger. Once these have been established in this way, let us observe which numbers arise from addition, multiplication, or division of them with one another. For example, twelve arises from the addition of one to eleven, two to ten, three to nine, four to eight, six to six, seven to five. In multiplication, however, twelve is produced from the multiplication of four by three, or of two by six. In division we have twelve if we divide twenty-four by two. Further, when the fingers are merely raised, it signifies addition; but when we touch one with another, multiplication. But if we bend one and raise the other, division must be understood.

Therefore, wishing to demonstrate the letter m, which occupies the twelfth place, I indicate twelve either by addition, or by multiplication, or by division. First, by raising the two little fingers of each hand together with the thumb of the left hand; for the thumb signifies one, while one of the fingers denotes five and the other six; but five, six, and one make twelve, which number indicates the letter m. By multiplication in this way: let us touch the third finger from the thumb of the left hand with the index finger of the right, since three multiplied by four makes twelve; or let us touch the little finger of the right hand with the index finger of the left, because the same [unclear] six twice gives twelve. It could also be done in another way, namely by the contact of the index finger of the right hand and the middle finger of the left, which show six. These again, by contact of both thumbs, or of the right index finger and the left thumb, signify the multiplication of the former number by two; but twice six makes twelve.

By division thus: first we shall indicate twenty-four, the division of which number by two yields twelve. Division by two is represented by the gesture of which I spoke above, namely, if two thumbs are shown, one indeed raised and the other bent; likewise the thumb and little finger of the left hand, while the index finger of the right is inclined. For they signify the partition of six by three, that is, two; by these, twenty-four divided demonstrates twelve. So much concerning dactylogy, or the speech of the fingers, which can also be handled otherwise in infinite ways, by assigning to fixed places vowels, consonants, semivowels, double letters, liquids, and treating such matters as shall seem good to each person. Although these things may appear ridiculous, nevertheless they have very great use if by a certain analogy they are transferred to other matters. Moreover, there are some things of which the author makes mention partly in the exposition of this passage, partly toward the end; but because they pertain to the treatment of steganography, let them be postponed for the present until that point has been reached.
