Fuerunt qui accidentibus) Sententia est, quaecunque in uni uersa rerum natura sunt, siue ab intellectu, siue à sensibus percipiantur, in eum usum conuerti posse, ut eo modo quo uocabula significent. Hinc est quod animi nostri uoluntatem, infinitis modis occulte, citra suspitionem, &amp; alicuius hominis impedimentum alteri significare licet, per dictiones,</per per signa quae dictio nes notãt, ut per luce, per colores, umbras, sonos, odores, sapores, per qualitates quae tactum afficiunt, per figuras, magnitudines, numeros, per motum aut statum quarumcunque rerum, ut sunt partes corporis, per gestus digitorum, ocułorum nutius et c, Quae quidem omnia si recte tractentur, iuxtaq́; literas, sillabas, dictiones, orationes, certo ordine, & numeris adscriptis disposita fuerint, admirandas facultates hominibus praestant, & tantò excellentiores quanto quis peritior ac exercitationi fuerit in ijs disciplinis, quae circa principia, causas et accidentia sensibilium uersantur. Talis est Catoptrice, quae docet uisibilia rerum signa in momento referre uisui, per certas imagines procul à nobis extra speacula in aërem proiectas, & ad significãdam aliquam orationem institutas, quas facile intelligit, qui signorũ cognitionem habet. Caeterum quo pacto fieri possit, ut omnia ad signum usum transferantur, non est huius instittuti, sed ad steganographiam pertinet, cuius operis argumenta, doctißimus uir Iohannes Trithemius in quadam epistola ad Bostium his uerbis recenset, etc. In manibus iam habeo grande opus, quod si unquam fuerit publicatum, quod absit, totus mũdus mirabitur, cuius primi libri titulus est Steganographia. Erunt autem quatuoꝵ libri, quilibet ad minus centum capitulis diltinguetur. Incepi hoc opus ad instantiant uniuꝰ magni principis quem nominare non opus est, quaeris quid hoc opus docet? Maxima docet, omnibuisq́; nescientibus stupenda et incredibilia, quae à seculo nunquam sunt audita. Primus enim liber continet plusquam centum modos occulte scribendi, quicquid uelis sine omni suspitione, sine literarum transpositione, sine omni timore, ita ut nō sit homo in mundo, qui naturali industria scire uel suspicari quidẽ poßit, quid in meis literis contineatur praeter eũ qui artem nouit ex me, uel ex eo quem ego docuero. Verba sunt, plana et familiaria, omni suspicione carentia, sed intentionem meam nemo sinc arte percipere poterit in aeternum, quantuncunque fit doctus, et est resuerè stupenda. Secundus liber multo mirabiliora continebit, per quem uideliꝺicti in hac arte possum mentis meae conceptum notum facere artem mean.

They say that, when its milk is used to write on the body, if ash is sprinkled on, the letters appear”; and thus, indeed, they preferred to address adulteresses rather than by little notes.

The second kind, Hyphasmaticon. The very learned Theodorus Bibliander has “hyphalmicon,” for this reason, as I think: because in this sort of concealment none of the letters appears before the paper has been immersed in water. Thus, when we write letters with alum, water poured over the paper will make it darker than the letters, which otherwise could not have been read.

Letters are also written in various ways. Herodotus, near the end of book seven: After Xerxes had resolved to undertake an expedition against Greece, Demaratus, who was at Susa, when he had learned this, judged that it should be reported to the Greeks. But since he could not do it otherwise, for it was dangerous lest he be detected, he devised this thing: taking a pair of writing-tablets, he scraped the wax from them. Then on the wood of them he scratched the king’s plan. When he had scratched it in letters, he covered it again with wax, so that the tablets would present no business to the road-guards for the person to whom they were being carried. When these had been brought to Lacedaemon, the Lacedaemonians could not interpret them until, as I understand it, Gorgo, daughter of Cleomenes and wife of Leonidas, warned them, herself interpreting the matter, ordering the wax to be broken off; for they would find letters in the wood. So the Lacedaemonians, listening to her, found the letters, read them over, and then sent them on to the Greeks.

Gellius, book seventeen, chapter 9: “There is also,” he says, “in the records of Greek affairs a certain deep and hard-to-grasp hiding-place, devised with barbarian cunning.” There was a man named Histiaeus, born in a not undistinguished place in the land of Asia. At that time King Darius held Asia under his rule. This Histiaeus, when he was in Persia with Darius, wished to announce certain secret matters to a certain Aristagoras by clandestine writing. He devised this remarkable concealment of letters: from his slave, who had long had diseased eyes, he shaved the hair from the whole head as though for the sake of treating him, and marked his bare head in the forms of letters. With these letters he wrote out what he had wished. Afterwards he kept the man at home until his hair grew back. When this had happened, he ordered him to go to Aristagoras. “And when you come to him,” he said, “say that I have commanded him to shave your head, just as I myself recently did.” The slave came to Aristagoras as he had been ordered and brought his master’s instruction. And he, thinking that this order was not without purpose, did what had been commanded; thus the letters were carried through.

Herodotus writes almost the same things; in that author it is also read in book one: When Astyages was harsh toward the Medes, Harpagus, insinuating himself with each of them individually, persuaded the leading men that Astyages ought to be removed from the kingship, with Cyrus chosen. When these matters had been arranged and prepared by Harpagus, then at last, wishing to reveal his intention to Cyrus, who was staying among the Persians, and being unable to do so otherwise, since the roads were guarded, he devised a thing of this sort: having gutted a hare, which he had skilfully obtained, so that nothing at all was cut away, he put inside it a little book in which he had written whatever he pleased; and, having sewn up the belly, he handed the hare, together with the nets, to a certain hunter of his household, a man of greatest trustworthiness, instructing him by word of mouth that, when he gave the hare, he should tell Cyrus to open it with his own hands and to do so without witnesses. He sent the man away into Persia. When the messenger had carried this out, Cyrus received the hare, opened it, found the little book that was in it, and read it. See Justin, book 1.

The historians also report that doves served as messengers in difficult circumstances, so that Hirtius the consul sent letters tied to their necks or feet to Decimus Brutus during the siege of Mutina, and Decimus Brutus sent them to Hirtius, after he had arranged food in certain very high places and had taught doves, previously shut up in darkness and worn down by much hunger, to fly back and forth.

Some, in order to avoid suspicion, write on paper with ink, [as if?] they wished to communicate something to a friend about domestic matters; afterwards they write what is secret with urine in the spaces. Others use the juice of lemons or onions; others use pounded sal ammoniac with water poured over it. Things written with letters of this kind are completely hidden before they have been brought near the fire. Some follow the poet’s counsel: “Since he can hide papers bound to his leg, / And jun[unclear].”

Haec ideo dixerim, ut si forte aliquādo rumor ad te p̄uenerit, me aut scire aut posse miranda, non me magum dico existimares, sed philosophū Nā ꝙ Alberto magno ꝓfudißimo rerũ naturaliū scrutatori cõtigit ut ꝓpter mirãda quae occulta uirtute naturae operatus est magus à uulgo sit habitus, mihi sũ cer tus similiter cõtingere posse, si queris unde mihi ista que nemo alius nouit audi. Nō ab homine neque p̃ hominẽ ista didici, sed p̄ reuelatione nescio cu ius, cũ enim pręsenti anno quadāuice cogitarē quid noui possem inuenire ꝙ omnes lateret, coepi cogitare si ea possem excogitare, quaedixi mirada. Cũ post longā phantasiā tanꝗ de re impoßibili penitus desperarē, dormi tũ ea me nocte reposui, fatuitatē meā ipse mecũ deridens quā impoßibilia quaerere tētauerim. Eadē nocte astitit mihi quidā dicēs, nō sunt uana o Tri temi, quae cogitasti quāꝗ tibi sint imposabilia, quae nec tu nec alius tecum poteris inuenire dixiq́; ad eũ. Si ergo possibia sunt, dic obsecro quomo- do fiãt. Et aperiés os suũ, de singulis ꝑ ordinē docuit, ostendês quomo- do fieri, que multis diebus frustra cogitauerã, de facili posset. Ecce co- rã deo quia nõ mētior sed ueritatẽ dico neminē ista adhuc docui, q̃uis mul ti ꝓmittētes magna, sepe rogarint, pręter unũ principē cui scribo, quem de poßibilitate artis manifesto argumēto feci certiorē, nec decet ista alios scire, q̃ principes, alioquin multa per ea fierēt mala, traditiões, deceptio nes, fornicationes, & alia quaecũque uellēt homines mali. Sed bene utentes arte multa per eam bona reipublicae facere possent, poßum autem ista om nia docere in omni lingua totius mundi quā nunquā audiui. Hec tibi Bostĩ propterea significare uolui, ne me crederes ociosum. Hactenus uerba Trithemij. Postremo sunt aliae ingentes utilitates ho- rum librorũ polygraphie, quas in libros nostris de ratione docendi et di- scedi tractabimus, qualiacũque enim haec uideantur, tamen plus habent in receffu quam in fronte promittunt. And to carry gentle marks beneath the joined foot. Let the guardian beware of these; instead of paper let the knowing back present itself, and let it bear words on its own body. There are also other devices: for instance, they paint letters on flint with the fat of a goat or ox; when it has been placed in vinegar for several hours and then taken out again, it displays to sight what had been inscribed. Likewise, they write with the white of an egg and dip it into ink; when this is scraped off, the letters are seen. Finally, in this place he wraps many things in obscure words, and in words by no means received in common use, lest he give perverse men an opportunity either to abuse these things or to devise worse ones. He wrote “race” with the true syllables for “cera,” just as “Roma” for “amor,” “nemilua” for “alumine,” “raphocam” for “camphora,” and so on. But since such matters, for the public good, must be handled rather sparingly and do not pertain to our undertaking, let us omit explaining everything; for it is enough if it is understood what he meant to signify by this third kind of letters.

There were also, as Bede bears witness) The sense is: the ancients not only wrote or spoke with words, as we do, but also transferred whatever the world contains, and whatever can be grasped by us, to signify things by a certain definite art. Diodorus Siculus, in book four, says: “The letters of the Egyptians closely resemble various living creatures, extremities, and those of human beings and instruments, but especially those of craftsmen; for their words are expressed not by the composition of syllables or by letters, but by the form of images, through their signification handed down to men’s memory by use.” They write, for example, a hawk, a crocodile, a serpent, a human eye, hands, a face, and other things of this kind. The hawk denotes a thing quickly done, since this bird is almost the swiftest of all; this notation is transferred to domestic affairs that are done swiftly. The crocodile signifies evil. The eye is interpreted as the preserver of justice and the guardian of the whole body. Of the remaining parts of the body, the right hand with fingers spread signifies freedom, but the left with them compressed signifies tenacity and avarice. In the same way the form of the other parts of the body and instruments denoted something definite; and those who had observed these things by memory, long use, and meditation immediately recognized what they expressed. Petrus Crinitus also, in book [unclear], chapter 2, writes that this kind of method of writing existed among the Egyptians. Concerning the letters of the Egyptians which are called hieroglyphic, not only is there mention among the ancient authors, but this can still be observed on obelisks, on which those figures and images of different animals, herbs, rivers, and trees, sculpted there, designate the philosophy of that nation, as Strabo and Pliny, most weighty authors, testify. For on the obelisks of Kings Sesostris and Sennosornis, which were brought from Egypt to the city, the interpretation of the nature of things is marked by symbols of this sort and by hieroglyphic signs. For thus the philosophy of the Egyptians is believed to have first been illustrated, as is handed down by the same Pliny and by others. Among other images, they were accustomed to mark scarabs, bees, rivers, oxen, vultures, and other things of that kind. Moreover, from the very image of the bee the symbol of a king was signified, because in performing the duties of life he ought to have no less the sting of justice than the sweet clemency of honey. In the vulture they indicated the genius and majesty of nature, because among these birds only females are found, etc. They also painted many other signs in place of words; on these see Horapollo on hieroglyphic letters; Pliny, book 36, chapter 8, and also chapter 12, where, according to the more correct reading, “Sesostris” is found for “Sesotidis,” and “Nuncoreus Pharaoh” for [unclear]. Moreover, Strabo, book 17; Cornelius Tacitus, book 13; Coelius Rhodiginus, Ancient Readings, book 29, chapter 26; and Volaterranus, book 33, mention letters of this sort, although he writes that they have as yet been discovered by no one.

by means of signs that indicate words, as by light, by colors, shadows, sounds, odors, tastes, by qualities that affect touch, by shapes, magnitudes, numbers, by the motion or position of any things whatever, such as parts of the body, by gestures of the fingers, nods of the eyes, etc. All these things, indeed, if they are handled properly and, according to letters, syllables, words, and sentences, have been arranged in a fixed order and with numbers assigned to them, furnish men with wonderful capacities, and the more excellent in proportion as one is more skilled and practiced in those disciplines that deal with the principles, causes, and accidents of sensible things. Such is Catoptrics, which teaches how to present visible signs of things to the sight in a moment, by means of certain images projected far from us out of mirrors into the air, and devised to signify some discourse; these are easily understood by one who has knowledge of the signs. But in what way it may be possible for all things to be transferred to the use of signs is not part of the present undertaking, but belongs to steganography; the subjects of that work the most learned man Johannes Trithemius lists in a certain letter to Bostius in these words, etc.

I already have in hand a great work which, if it is ever published, which God forbid, the whole world will marvel at; the title of its first book is Steganography. There will be four books, and each will be divided into at least one hundred chapters. I began this work at the insistence of a certain great prince, whom there is no need to name. You ask what this work teaches? It teaches very great things, astonishing and incredible to all who do not know them, things that have never been heard of since the beginning of the world. For the first book contains more than one hundred methods of writing secretly whatever you wish, without any suspicion, without transposition of letters, without any fear, so that there is no man in the world who by natural ingenuity could know, or even suspect, what is contained in my letters, except the man who knows the art from me, or from him whom I shall have taught. The words are plain and familiar, devoid of all suspicion, but no one without the art will ever be able to perceive my intention, however learned he may be; and the thing is truly astonishing. The second book will contain much more wonderful things, by which, namely, [unclear] in this art I can make known the conception of my mind [unclear].

to one who knows [the art], at any distance whatever, to a hundred miles or more, safely, without words, without writings, without signs, through any messenger whatsoever; and if he has been seized on the road, if he has been questioned even under the harshest tortures, he can disclose nothing about my message, because he knows absolutely nothing about it. Whatever may happen, my message will always remain hidden, nor could all the men of the whole world, if they were gathered together at once, track it down by natural power. This too I can do without a messenger whenever I wish; I can also make my will known, even when long absent, to one sitting in prison who knows the art, however closely he is guarded, even if he were sitting three miles under the earth. And all these things, most broadly and universally, whenever and as often as I wish, I can do naturally, without any superstition or aid of any spirits whatsoever.

They are wonderful things, I admit; but hear things more wonderful. The third book teaches an art by which I can, in two hours, teach a man who knows that same knowledge and only his mother tongue, and who has never known a word of Latin speech, to write, read, and understand Latin fairly elegantly and fluently, as much as he wishes, so that whoever sees his letters will praise the words and will understand them as composed in Latin. The fourth book contains many astonishing experiments, but purely natural ones. Namely, I can make known my mind to one who knows [the art] [unclear] whenever I wish, even while speaking, preaching, playing the organ, or singing, without hindrance to any other action whatsoever, so that while preaching good and holy things I may make known, not by words, not by signs, to anyone who knows [the art], most broadly, whatever I wish, even with closed eyes; and the fourth book will contain many other secrets which are not to be brought before the public.

All who hear these things marvel at them; among them are many noble and very learned men, who think that these things are either impossible or wholly supernatural. To them, and to you, I answer what I have answered to many: that many things are naturally possible which, to those who do not know the powers of nature, seem impossible, or even supernatural. And behold, I speak before my God, who knows all things, that the wondrous things which I have stated above are much more excellent, deeper, and greater than I can write or you can believe; and yet all are purely natural, without any deception, without superstition, without magical art, without invocation or service of any spirits whatsoever. I have said these things for this reason: that if perhaps at some time a rumor should reach you that I either know or can do wonderful things, you should not, I say, think me a magician, but a philosopher. For what happened to Albertus Magnus, that most profound investigator of natural things, namely that because of the wonders which he performed by the hidden power of nature he was considered a magician by the common people, I am certain could likewise happen to me.

If you ask whence I have these things which no one else knows, hear: I learned these things not from man nor through man, but by revelation from I know not whom. For when in the present year I was once thinking what new thing I could discover that would be hidden from everyone, I began to consider whether I could devise those wonderful things which I have mentioned. When, after long imagining, I utterly despaired of it as an impossible matter, I laid myself down to sleep that night, laughing at my own folly within myself, that I had tried to seek impossible things. That same night someone stood by me, saying, “The things you have thought, O Trithemius, are not vain, although they are impossible for you, and neither you nor another with you will be able to discover them.” And I said to him: “If therefore they are possible, tell me, I beg, how they are done.” And opening his mouth, he taught me each thing in order, showing how what I had vainly pondered for many days could easily be done.

Behold, before God, because I do not lie but speak the truth: I have taught these things to no one yet, although many, promising great things, have often asked, except one prince to whom I am writing, whom I have made more certain of the possibility of the art by evident proof. Nor is it fitting for others to know these things than princes; otherwise many evils would be done through them: betrayals, deceptions, fornications, and whatever else evil men might wish. But those using the art well could do many good things for the commonwealth through it. Moreover I can teach all these things in every language of the whole world which I have never heard. I wanted to tell you these things, Bostius, so that you would not think me idle.

Thus far the words of Trithemius. Lastly, there are other immense uses of these books of Polygraphy, which we shall treat in our books On the Method of Teaching and Learning; for whatever these things may seem to be, they have more in reserve than they promise on the surface. Concerning Steganography, in whose first books hidden matters lie concealed, God willing, we shall deal separately.

[unclear] serve the secrets in every respect. The paraphrases, however, have been arranged so artfully that they produce a wholly Latin discourse, if only one is taken from each order. And it should be noted that, by reason of our German speech, the twenty-fourth letter W is taken at the end of the alphabet, since all the remaining letters perform service for both languages. We have set the co-signifying words in such order by this method that, whichever you take from each line, once the total calculation has been made, agreement will remain. Yet caution is needed, so that from any line of syntax you take only one, and so that no monad does injury to the binary. Care must also be taken that, as often as you approach the cabalistic operation, you first count all and each of the minutes of the night, and join them in due proportion to the degrees of the following day. But if, by the arcane arrangement, the minutes do not suffice to the degrees of the day right to the end, the windy runner must by prudent counsel be brought back to the arch-measurer. Nor is it an obstacle if by chance the night falls upon the head of the day, since the prudent operator in the art can withdraw from the front by voluntary addition by as much as he sees the night exceed the light of day. And this is to be understood throughout the whole work of the Polygraphy concerning the individual chapters. Yet we say that this consideration must be assigned to unity, by which the binary may be certified by the indicator of note-reversion, lest it happen to go astray. By the established rule the binary will stand from the monad, and the monad is produced. Nothing is put here in vain; nothing is cited without cause or idly. Therefore we necessarily warn everyone who wishes to transcribe this work of our Polygraphy, either wholly or in part, to take diligent care above all that he does not depart in any respect from our archetype, that he does not skip, neglect, or transpose any word whatever. Indeed, if he omits a letter or word in substantials, if he changes a word contrary to its nature, he has made the procedure of the whole work useless. Therefore let him either transcribe it properly, or not transcribe it.

There follow the words of the first order, with minutes, for the degrees.

FINEM adesse libri Polygraphiae nostrae primi gaudemus, quo ad ea quae restant promptiores effecti, quae sint ingenij uires iudicamus tentandum. Turbant enim nonnunquam nouiter inuenta principia tem, quia quem sequuntur omnes neminem habet praecedentem. Grauior est cuiuslibet adinuentionis inceptio prima, quae postea quam solidata fue= rit, maiorem authori confidentiam adducit. Primum itaque librum adin= uentionis nostrae cum Dei fauore et auxilio absoluentes, trecentis octo= ginta quatuor minucijs distinximus totum, proprios gradus periphrasma= tum singulis per ordinem ut cernitur supponentes. Et ista Christianum satis pulchrum formant concentum, sexdecim stationes uiarias, ducentis supra nouem phraseon milibus rite per omnia coniunctis. Nihil hic deest harum adinuentionum nostrarum studiosis, quo minus in rebus misticis, se cretis et arcanis, etiam remotius tutißime nunciandis plenißimam ha= beant scientiam et facultatem. Omnia quae artis continentur in orbe et puncto procedunt, quorum athomi lineam constituunt orbicularem, & lu= minis multitudine rectam. Quicquid extra lineam est, diei communi ra= tione deseruit, non nocti. Nox enim terminos minutiarum et paraphra seon semper inclusa nunquam egreditur. Quotiens igitur cunque lineam rectam diei transieris, & nocturnae syntaxeseos propositum non impleue ris, caput retorque as ad caudam, & colligatione facta fiat ligamentum utriusq́; adiuicem Vmbram sic ordina, ut solem non confundat similitudi ne uocis Nec reuereare pudorem, si prima calculatione dies non comprae= henderit umbram, sed linearum diei minucias studiose consydera, alteram cum altera cõnumera, donec proportio necessaria ad uotum subsequatur Poteris etiam a primo saltum facere in secundum, sciens quod in prima creatione dierum factum est uespere et mane dies unus Verum quo hanc uespere consummato, diem reduc in sequentem, & signo dato per pun= ctum binario simul et monadi notum fige mysterium. Verum quo hanc cuitare difficultatem poßis, orbis nostri totius, magnas reuolutiones per gradus distingue arithmaticos, & ubi dies pro nocte repetitur, notam Ar chimedis impone uolanti, ne ternarius immaturus reditum ad unitatem biq B b nario intercludat Nam propterea minutias singulis gradibus artificiosa inuentione praeposuimus, ut in his operantẽ à labore numerãdi paraphras mata leuaremus. Si fueris industrius, diligens et studiosus in his quae ut ar tis principia nouae tradidimus, crede nobis maiora inuenies latentia quam nos polliciti sumus. Enimuero cum inhis naturalia plura contineantur ar cana, unum scias non ultimum, quod methateseos operatione prudenti, e- tiamcum uoles peritißimum in hac arte facies ignarum, uidentem coecum, &amp; doctum imperitum. Si falsa Hebraeorum esset uera opinio, orbium decem et amp; octo milium hominibus singulis, ista adiuuentio no- stra singulos daret modos tuto et amp; secretè scri- bendi ac nunciandi latißime quae- cunqꝫ latine uellent arcana. Aer et ignis, aqua et amp; terra, fontes et amp; flumina, arbores et amp; fructeꝫ, flores et amp; gramina, uerba et amp; nomina, accidens et amp; substantia, lapides et amp; arena, fimus et amp; stercora, res et amp; uocabula, honesta et amp; uerecun da, ligna et amp; metalla, dura et amp; liquida, existentia et amp; non existentia, histoc= ria et amp; fabula, bestiae et amp; bruta, homines et amp; iumenta, singula et amp; uniuersa, quae uel sermo potest exprimere, uel anima cogitare, campum Polygra= phiae nostrae pręstant latißimum, &amp; artem quantum mortalibus potest constare promittunt ampliandam fore in infinitum. We rejoice that the end of the first book of our Polygraphia is at hand; made readier by it for what remains, we judge that it must be tried what the powers of our intellect are. For newly discovered principles sometimes disturb the mind, since he whom all follow has no one preceding him. The first beginning of any invention is the more difficult; after it has been made firm, it brings greater confidence to its author. Therefore, completing with God’s favor and help the first book of our invention, we have divided the whole into 384 minutiae, placing beneath each, in order as is seen, the proper degrees of the periphrases. And these form a sufficiently beautiful Christian concord: sixteen way-stations, with more than 209,000 phrases duly joined in all respects. Nothing is lacking here for students of these inventions of ours, so that in mystical, secret, and hidden matters, even to be reported very remotely and most safely, they may have the fullest knowledge and faculty.

All things contained in the art proceed in the circle and the point, whose atoms constitute a circular line, and, by the multitude of light, a straight one. Whatever is outside the line serves the common reckoning of day, not night. For night, always enclosed, never passes beyond the limits of the minutiae and paraphrases. Therefore, as often as you cross the straight line of day and do not fulfill the proposed plan of nocturnal syntax, turn the head back to the tail, and when a joining has been made, let there be a binding of each to the other. Arrange the shadow so that it does not confuse the sun by similarity of sound. And do not be ashamed if in the first calculation the day has not comprehended the shadow; rather, consider carefully the minutiae of the lines of day, reckon one together with another, until the necessary proportion follows according to your wish. You will also be able to make a leap from the first to the second, knowing that in the first creation of days there was made evening and morning, one day. But when this evening has been completed, bring the day back into the following one, and, when the sign has been given through the point known simultaneously to the binary and the monad, fix the mystery. But so that you may be able to avoid this difficulty, distinguish the great revolutions of our whole circle by arithmetical degrees; and where day is repeated for night, set the mark of Archimedes upon the flying thing, lest an immature ternary block the return to unity for the binary.

For this reason we have placed minutiae before the individual degrees by an artful invention, so that in these we might relieve the worker from the labor of counting the paraphrases. If you are industrious, diligent, and studious in these things which we have handed down as the principles of a new art, believe us: you will find greater things hidden than we have promised. Indeed, since many natural secrets are contained in these matters, know this one thing, not least: that by the prudent operation of metathesis, even when you wish, you will make the most skilled man in this art ignorant, the seeing blind, and the learned unskilled. If the false opinion of the Hebrews were true, for each person of the eighteen thousand worlds this invention of ours would give individual modes of safely and secretly writing and reporting, most widely, whatever Latin secrets they wished.

End of the First Book of the Polygraphia.

The Second Book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Peapolis, of the Order of Saint Benedict, begins.

The method of numbering mortals, by art imitating nature, admits no reckoning of the monad. Hence, although the arrangement of the preceding book of the Polygraphy, through the extension and metathesis of particulars, is, as it were, sufficient for the universals of this art in the infinite progressions of number, nevertheless a certain consideration has moved us to join one to the other. The condition of light is different in each; but night in both preserves inviolate the order of its course. The prudent reader, from these small inventions of ours, and not polished sufficiently to the exact rule, will easily be able, if he is strong in excellent talent, to discover greater and more polished ones. Whatever is visible, set within the whole circuit of the world, readily provides support for the service of this new art of ours. Air and fire, water and earth, springs and rivers, trees and fruits, flowers and grasses, words and names, accident and substance, stones and sand, dung and filth, things and terms, honorable and modest things, wood and metals, hard and liquid things, things existing and not existing, history and fable, beasts and brute animals, men and beasts of burden, each and all things which either speech can express or the soul can think, furnish a very wide field for our Polygraphy, and promise that, so far as it can be established among mortals, the art will be enlarged infinitely. For just as from unity, through the binary, the ternary generates a perfect number in the quaternary, so the consummation of this invention, through the quaternary, establishing its root in the twice-perfect binary, gives us an infinite number under the [unclear] of things and paraphrases of Polygraphy. For even if among us all our things are terminable, nevertheless many things often occur which, because of the slowness of our understanding, seem to us infinite. Who will be able to count the drops of the sea? And who will penetrate the inscrutable heart of man? Just as a finite and circumscribable number can, by progression, be led into infinity, so the arrangement of this art is enlarged to immensity by varied metathesis. Whatever is seen anywhere in the whole world is in every way conformed to our arrangement, nor is anything known to us which is devoid of mystery, if the method is understood from a master. But we, persuaded by reason, have halted under the service of the binary, and briefly explain the smallest part of the whole. Nor is occasion given to us to raise what has been begun to weightier matters; if it is offered to us acceptably, we shall not refuse to make better things manifest to those who desire them. For it is written: Where there is no hearing, never pour forth speech. Therefore, adding the second book of the Polygraphy to the first, we keep the same form of method: in the light of day, three hundred and eight paraphrases of the simple, which, if suitable time had been present, we could have given more elegantly, with sufficient broadening, wider in the open field. But studious posterity will easily provide both, adding brightness to the matter and sufficient progress to the form. The first inventor of any art transmits greater things to posterity, because, since the beginnings of an art are hard and unfamiliar, no subtle invention is found completed from its origin. From Peapolis, which is Herbipolis, a city of the Eastern Franks, on the twelfth day of the month of February, in the year of the Lord 1508.

Vxiliante domino nostro Iesu Christo, saluator fidelium animarum, qui sacro uiuit in unitate ternario cum patre et spiritu sancto, trinus in personis, & unus in substantia deus, incomprehensibiles, omnipotēs et sempiternus: à quo, in quo, et per quē omne bonū pulchrum procedit et uerum, secundum hunc Polygraphiae librum perduximus ad finem. De quo ipsi laus, honor, uirtus et gloria: qui per mortis suae innocentiam genus nostrum de interitu perditionis aeternae liberauit, & omnibus in eum conscientia pura credentibus, aeternae uitae aditum miseratione perpetua rescravit Lineatim octo et trecenta paraphrasmata consignamus, prolixiorem euagationem consilio deuitantes. Satis etenim nobis in huius lucubrationis exordiouisum est, si causam uolentibus ampliora dederimus perquirendi, cum nobis ad ea defuerit et tempus et ratio. Lector amice uale. Ex Peapoli, penultima die mensis Februarij. Anno domini Millesimo quingentesimo octavo. FINIS LIBRI SECVNDI Polygraphiae. IOANNIS TRITEMII ABBATIS PEAPO, LITANI ORDINIS SANCTI BENEDICTI, LI. ber Polygraphiae Tertius initis tium sumit. mutantur animi, uariantur et uestes: linguarum alteratur simplicitis, & prisca uariatur idiomatum proprietas, & nihil stable reperitur in huma= nis. Omnum enim uicissitudin est rerum, & succedit uarietas simplicitati animorum. Quis de fluentiam hanc, ut ita loquar, perpetuam ad concor= diam poterit reducere unitatis? Transeunt enim tempora ut scriptu ra dicit, & multiplex erit scientia. Quid autem duobus Polygraphiae li= bris praecedentibus tertium adjicimus, ratione non caruit speciali. Nam ut cum uariae sint hominum uoluntas, recte multiples dantur modi ad ho= nestas operationes In illis noctem dies illuminat, in istis uero dies à lumine uacat. Illic umbram lux circumducit in lumine, isthic autem caecus caecum il= luminat, & uisum sine oculis existens et permanens quem non habet tene= bris ministrat. Hic nox diem caligine perpetua obnubilat, & ambulans in tenebris sine lumine caeco ducatum praestat. Haec paraphrasmata cunctis per mundum hominibus deseruiunt, & in omni lingua quodlibet archanum tuto, secure, ac sine periculo ad cabalisticum binarium transmittunt. Bar= baris risum mouet latinitas, et suspicionem latinis ipsa barbaries generat. Refert tamẽ nihil aut parum quoniam suspicio quantumlibet fuerit, mysto rium nihilominus omne secretissimum continebit. Ad mentem regulas et praecepta quae tradidimus operator studiosus reuocet, ne inutiliter et inua num sibi et alijs laboret. Intelligentia enim opus est, sine qua nullius artis constabit utilitas. Iter paucis ostendimus ad maxima, & finitis modum dedimus ad infinita Ex datis et acceptis, facile maiora parantur a micis. Lector memento notam retrogradam in omni loco pos se configi, quo usque notam approehendas quietis. Vale, Ex Peapoli, prima die Martij. Anno domini M.D.VIII. With the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, savior of faithful souls, who lives in the sacred ternary unity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, threefold in persons and one God in substance, incomprehensible, almighty, and everlasting, from whom, in whom, and through whom every good, beautiful, and true thing proceeds, we have brought this second book of the Polygraphy to its end. To him be praise, honor, power, and glory: he who through the innocence of his death freed our race from the destruction of eternal perdition, and in perpetual mercy opened again the entrance to eternal life for all who believe in him with a pure conscience. We set down, line by line, three hundred and eight paraphrases, deliberately avoiding more lengthy digression. For at the beginning of this night-work it seemed enough to us if we gave to those who wished it a reason for seeking out fuller things, since both time and method were lacking to us for them. Farewell, friendly reader. From [Peapolis?], on the penultimate day of the month of February, in the year of the Lord 1508.

END OF THE SECOND BOOK of the Polygraphy.

The third book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of [Peapolis?], of the Order of Saint Benedict, begins.

What, from the beginning of human creation, confounded the unity of language? Was it not the division of bodies and the variety of minds? For as Truth declares in the Gospel: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. For the tongue is the instrument for bringing outward those conceptions which the mind has thought within itself in its inner parts. Yet there are several modes of this service of the mind’s secrets to sense, whose properties vary both by use and by art. Use, introduced at will, is common to many; art, however, to few. Finally, even the unregulated use of speaking itself, how much it has varied among the Theutons alone in six hundred years, no one will readily estimate who has not rather often reread Otfried, the monk of Weissenburg, in his poems in the German language. The sea flows and ebbs; human beings, once dying, do not return again to the present life. Customs succeed customs, and the vigor of mortal minds always falls away toward softer things. Who today among the Germans, the ancient imitators of the Greeks, retains knowledge of the old idioms? In chronicles and old histories of the Franks, Hunibald, Doracus, and the other writers who preceded us by a thousand years mixed into their compositions many things spoken both in ancient verse and in prose of the Theutonic language, which today are understood by few. Why do I speak of ancient times, when our own proper idiom among the East Franks, Swabians, Bavarians, Rhinelanders, Mosellans, Cologne people, Saxons, and Thuringians undergoes notable variation every day? Human beings change over time, and customs vary,

Minds change, and garments too are varied; the simplicity of languages is altered, the ancient character of idioms is varied, and nothing stable is found among human things. For there is a change of all things, and variety succeeds to the simplicity of minds. Who will be able to reduce this perpetual flowing-away, so to speak, to the concord of unity? For times pass away, as Scripture says, and knowledge will be manifold. But the fact that we add a third book to the two preceding books of the Polygraphy has not lacked a special reason. For, since human wills are various, multiple methods are rightly given for honorable operations. In those, day illumines night; in these, however, day lacks light. There light leads shadow about in light; here, however, the blind illumines the blind, and, being and remaining sight without eyes, supplies to darkness what it does not have. Here night darkens day with perpetual gloom, and, walking in darkness without light, gives guidance to the blind. These paraphrases serve all people throughout the world, and in every language safely, securely, and without danger transmit any secret whatever to the cabalistic binary. Latin moves barbarians to laughter, and barbarism itself produces suspicion among Latins. Yet it matters nothing, or little, since suspicion, however great it may have been, will nevertheless contain every most secret mystery. Let the diligent operator recall to mind the rules and precepts that we have handed down, lest he labor uselessly and in vain for himself and for others. For understanding is needed, without which the usefulness of no art will stand. In a few words we have shown the path to the greatest things, and with finite things we have given a method for infinite things. From things given and received, greater things are easily prepared by friends. Reader, remember that the retrograde mark can be fixed in every place, until you apprehend the mark of rest.

Farewell. From [Peapoli?], on the first day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

Noctem arcanis tuto seruientem, umbris periphrasmatum ducendam commisimus, & numeros ordine quatuor linearum telotenus interposuimus pro usu uo= lentium adaptatos. Loca sunt minutiarum gradus habentia fixos tria milia centum quinquaginta, quanquã et horarum restent momẽta si volueris infi nita, pro secretandis in omni natione et lingua orbis quicquid arcani oc= currerit. Orbem linealiter nascentẽ ex puncto, quotiens nox imaginem lu cis excedit, quantum volueris: & opus fuerit reducere poteris ad semitam quaui nisti. Si noctis superest multum, reducito caudam draconis ad cau= dalicum originale in caput. Verum binarius omnino fit certificatus de notis et singnaculis unitatis Qui multum esurit, multũ laboret ut habeat quod manducet. Nec est opus magni laboris id quorum sum uolueris ducere, quod sua sponte progreditur. Hic ergo finem tertio Polygraphiae nostrae libro constituimus, in nomine patris et filij et Spiritus sancti. Lector mitis uale. Ex Peapoli, septima die mensis Martij. Anno domini ieisu Christi saluatoris millesimo quingentesimo octauo. Inditi= one undecima. FINIS LIBRI TERTII Polygraphiae. IOANNIS TRITEMII ABBATIS MONASTERII SANCTI IACOBI MAIORIS APOSTOLI Vurciburgensis, quondam Spanheimensis, ordinis diui Benedicti, quartus Polygraphiae liber incipit. ORDO expositulabat rationis quartum Polygraphie nostrae li- brum qualitate, inuentione et amp; facilitate dis imilem fieri pręcedentibus: quatenus uolentes rerum nostrarum participari arcanis non uno sed uarijs id modis asssequantur atque diuersis. Extendimus picam facilli ma inuentione compręhensibilem, ut nox per minutiam semper coniuncta monadi quolibet ordine in lunine cognoscatur diei. Nulla istic inter unitatem et amp; binarium reperitur dissensio: neque oportebit artis instrumentum operari uolentem habere ad manum, quando primę succedens sine medio, latens ostendit mysterium. Vnde prudens, intelligens et amp; expertus scientiam, omni tempore et amp; loco, satisfaciet operationi. Binarius ab unitate recipit, unde ternarium producit. Facilis est huius cryptologiae facie prima cognitio: posteà quam luna uel punto unico fuerit à sole illustrata. Quamus et amp; fieri possit quod gnosticus euadat industrius sine manuductione magistri. Quod in isto tamen libro tantum reor intelligendum, in precedentiū nullo De sequentibus autem suo dabitur iudicium. Inter omnes quos dedimus pręsentiatenus cabalisticus arcanorum modos, istius libri quarti progressus facilior in infinitum potest extendi. Quare sufficit me cupientibus ampliora formam tradidisse simul et amp; causam exempli. Lumen intelligentiae haec facile penetrat omnia. Scripsi Peapolis, nona die Martij, Anno domini M.D.Octauo.

What we promised at the beginning of the third book of our work, the Polygraphia, for attaining the shadow and likeness of a new gloss before the inexperienced, we have sufficiently supplied by way of example, with a saving of labor. We have entrusted night, safely serving secrets, to be guided by the shadows of circumlocutions, and we have inserted numbers in the order of four lines [unclear], adapted for the use of those who wish it. The places are degrees of minutes having fixed points, three thousand one hundred and fifty, although, if you wish, there remain infinite moments of hours for keeping secret, in every nation and language of the world, whatever secret matter may arise. The circle, arising linearly from a point, whenever night exceeds the image of light, you will be able to bring back, as much as you wish and as there is need, to whatever path you have striven after. If much of night remains, bring the dragon’s tail back to the original tail-place in the head. But the binary is made wholly certified by the marks and little signs of unity. He who hungers much, let him labor much, so that he may have something to eat. Nor is there need of great labor to lead that wherever you wish, since it proceeds of its own accord. Here, therefore, we set the end to the third book of our Polygraphia, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Gentle reader, farewell. From Peapoli, on the seventh day of the month of March, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior one thousand five hundred eight, in the eleventh indiction.

End of the Third Book of the Polygraphia.

The fourth book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Saint James the Greater, Apostle, at Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, of the order of Saint Benedict, begins.

Order of reasoning required that the fourth book of our Polygraphia be made unlike the preceding ones in quality, invention, and ease, so that those who wish to share in the secrets of our matters may attain this not by one method but by various and different ones. We have extended the magpie, comprehensible by a very easy invention, so that night, always joined through a minute to the monad in any order, may be recognized in the light of day. Here no disagreement is found between unity and the binary, nor will the person wishing to work the art need to have the instrument at hand, since what succeeds the first immediately, while hidden, shows the mystery. Hence the prudent man, understanding and experienced in the science, will satisfy the operation at every time and place. The binary receives from unity, whence it produces the ternary. The knowledge of this cryptology is easy at first sight, after the moon, or a single point, has been illuminated by the sun. And yet it may come to pass that the knowing man becomes skillful without the guidance of a master. I think, however, that this is to be understood only in this book, in none of the preceding ones. As for the following books, judgment will be given in its own place. Among all the cabalistic modes of secrets that we have given up to the present, the progression of this fourth book can more easily be extended to infinity. Therefore it is enough that I have handed down to those desiring fuller things both the form and the reason of the example.

The light of understanding easily penetrates all these things. I wrote at Peapoli, on the ninth day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

Minime quoque reor necessarium ea quae sunt recitata in precedentibus ad memoriam reducere, cum lector sagax si fuerit studiosus etiam quae in his maiora latitant possit auxiliante domino inuenire. Materiam sapienti et amp; studioso tradidimus si- mul et amp; causam quibus si prudenter uti uoluerit, suo nostrum ingenio supe- rabit Quisquis uero hanc stratam cupit in umbra pulchriorem, ingenio ma- num coniungat et amp; animũ, &amp; iter sibi faciat ipse paraphrasmate pulchrius decoratum. Memoria teneat fixum si quem ista delectant ut in orbe semper maneat praestituto, quem quolibet modo praetergressus fuerit, operatio to- ta inutilis euanescit. Hominum plura sunt nomina, sunt denique infinita pe- nè vocabula rerum, uillarum, ciuitatum, provinciarum, arbo- rum, lapidum et amp; uerborum, quae nostris omnia subseruiunt institutis. Ex his librium et amp; modum fieri constat non impoßibile, si cum diligentia sit pre- sto ingeniū, quae nostra inventa praecellant in infinitum. Qui uero tantae fuerit hebetudinis ut haec puerilia nostra intelligere nequeat, ea quae subti- liora restabunt quando penetrabit? Finem libro Polygraphiae quarto imponimus, cui quintum in nomine domini nostri Iesu Christi sociamus. FINIS LIBRI QVARTI Polygraphiae. IOHANNIS TRIHEMII ABBATIS SANCTI IACOBI APOSTOLI PEAPOLITANI. Polygraphiae Liber Quintus exordium capit. EA Quae auxiliante domino nostro Iesu Christo in quatuor praece= dentibus libris pro complemento Polygraphiae nostrae utcunque digęßimus, rationabiliter exigunt, ut reliqua huiuscem institutionis praecepta quae supersunt et amp; modos, breuiter in quinto pertractemus. Dabi mus itaqƺ modum in eo satis compendiosum per methatesin, id est, transpo sitionem literarum, quo securè, tuto, &amp; secretißimè amicus scribet ad a= micum quaecunqƺ uoluerit. Eo scribendi modo Caesařem Augustum legi= mus usum in arcanis. Qui quidem nunciãdi modus et si multipliciter sit se curus, semper tamen intuentibus habetur suspectus: quia mox ut litera= rum cernitur transpositio, qui curiosis est aliquid sub eis latere protinus suspicatur. Sunt autem modi huius adinuationis penè infiniti, è quibus nos prorecessaria introductione sequentes lectori praesignauimus, cuiusreliqua ingenio perscrutanda reseruamus. In primis ergo tabulam huiusindustriae premissius canonicam, cui alteram subscripsimus auersam. In hisduabus tabulis radix et amp; fundamentum memoratae transpositionis omninoponitur, super quo structura totius aedificij collocatur. His etenim duabustabulis rite cognitis et amp; intellectis, nulla transpositio litterarũ latere poterit, cum diligentia operantem. His quatuor et amp; uiginti alphabeta per ordinem coniunximus, ut lectori copiam transponendi grammata preberemus.Horum usus pro uoto consistit in singulis, aut si malueris etiam in uniuersis. Si tibi cum multis fuerit arcani cõmertium, alphabeta singula familiaribus tuis distribuc singulis, tu uero memoriae commenda quid unicuique. [unclear] d [unclear] tradideris· Primo quidem alphabetum committatur primũ, secundo secun dum: tertio tertium, & ita consequenter fiat de reliquis. Quod si prae mal titudine negotiorum aut familiae alphabeta quae signimus non sufficerẽt̃ ad omnia, uel si aliqua ex eis nimisuideantur patula et manifesta, uarias transpositiones nouas poterimus inducere, quarum et numerus fit maxi- mus, & arcani modui perpetuo maneat semper occultus. Cuius rei pona= mus exemplũ: B sit a,f sit b,l sit c,p sit d,t sit e,z sit f,c sit g,m sit h,& ita consequenter per totum alphabetum usuale fiat ut inter quamlibet li teram assumptam tres interiaceant ociose atque transpositae. Postea qua= tuor,deinde quinque,plures aut pauciores,ĩta tamen quod totum alphabe= tum quasi reuolutum in orbem concurrat, & litera nulla penitus obmitta= tur, sed unaquęque eadem serie pro alia in ordine suo collocetur· Quali= cũque modo scripseris ipsum aut memorie tenaciter noueris com mendandum,ne per obliuionem lapsus, quod scripseras ipse legere iam non poßis.Tot enim modis literarum transpositio uariari potest̃, quot se- cundum aestimationem intellectus humani qui operatione temporali conclu sus in corpore mortali non capit proprie infinita,mortalis consurget nume rus innumerabilis.Vnde quicunque modos scribendi per methatesin et plu res habere uoluerit et à nostra institutione remotos, si uel parum fuerit ingeniosus et diligens,facilem in operatione sua consequetur effectum. Maxima enim potest ingenium hõis si studio iuuetur et arte.Qui aūt sper nit minima,nunquam pertinget ad maiora.Scio plerosque futuros qui haec studia nostra ut uana et puerilia deridebunt,quibus damus pro re= sponso,nos omnino fore contentos modo illis complaceant, ad quorum sunt instantiam à nobis composita.· Sequitur tabula recta.

Now that the demonstration of the possibility of our new invention has been shown briefly, and no less sufficiently, I do not think that I myself should be wearied any longer on this same occasion, since the route and method extends to infinity, if anyone should need an example for further matters. Nor do I think it at all necessary to recall to memory the things that have been recited in the preceding sections, since the keen reader, if he is studious, will also be able, with the Lord’s help, to discover the greater things that lie hidden in these matters. We have handed over to the wise and studious man both the material and the cause; if he wishes to use them prudently, he will surpass us by his own talent. But whoever desires this path to be more beautiful in the shade, let him join hand and mind to talent, and let him make for himself a route more beautifully adorned by paraphrase. If these things delight anyone, let him keep it fixed in memory that he must always remain within the prescribed circle; if he passes beyond it in any way, the whole operation vanishes uselessly. There are many names of men; indeed there are almost infinite words for things, villages, cities, provinces, trees, stones, and words, all of which serve our purposes. From these it is clear that a book and a method can be made, not impossibly, if talent is present together with diligence, which may surpass our inventions infinitely. But he who is of such dullness that he cannot understand these childish things of ours, when will he penetrate the subtler things that remain? We set an end to the fourth book of the Polygraphy, to which we join the fifth, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

End of the Fourth Book of the Polygraphy.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James the Apostle at Wurzburg. The Fifth Book of the Polygraphia: the beginning.

Those things which, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have set forth, in whatever manner, in the four preceding books for the completion of our Polygraphia, reasonably require that we briefly treat, in the fifth, the remaining precepts and methods of this instruction which are left. Therefore in it we shall give a sufficiently concise method by metathesis, that is, by transposition of letters, by which a friend may write to a friend securely, safely, and most secretly whatever he wishes. We read that Caesar Augustus used this mode of writing in secret matters. And although this method of communication is secure in many ways, nevertheless it is always regarded with suspicion by those who look at it: for as soon as a transposition of letters is perceived, anyone curious at once suspects that something lies hidden beneath them. Now the methods of this invention are almost infinite; from them, for the necessary introduction, we have marked out the following for the reader, leaving the rest to be investigated by his own ingenuity. First, therefore, we have placed before him the canonical table of this craft, to which we have added beneath another, reversed one. In these two tables the root and foundation of the aforesaid transposition is wholly set down, upon which the structure of the whole edifice is placed. For when these two tables have been duly known and understood, no transposition of letters will be able to remain hidden from one working carefully. To these we have joined twenty-four alphabets in order, so that we might furnish the reader with an abundance for transposing letters. The use of these, according to one’s wish, consists in each single one, or, if you prefer, even in all of them. If you have secret dealings with many people, assign the individual alphabets to your individual intimates, and commit to memory what you have handed over to each.

Hand over the first alphabet to the first man, the second to the second, the third to the third, and so let it be done in sequence with the rest. But if, because of the multitude of affairs or of one’s household, the alphabets which we have marked out should not suffice for everything, or if some of them seem too open and plain, we shall be able to introduce various new transpositions, of which both the number is very great and the method of the secret may always remain perpetually hidden. Let us set down an example of this matter: let B be a, f be b, l be c, p be d, t be e, z be f, c be g, m be h, and so consequently let it be done through the whole usual alphabet, so that between any assumed letter three idle and transposed letters may intervene. Afterwards four, then five, more or fewer, yet in such a way that the whole alphabet, as though turned around in a circle, comes together, and no letter at all is omitted, but each is placed for another in its own order in the same series. In whatever way you have written it, it must be committed firmly to memory, lest, having fallen into forgetfulness, you yourself can no longer read what you had written. For the transposition of letters can be varied in as many ways as, according to the estimation of the human intellect, which, enclosed in a mortal body by temporal operation, does not properly grasp infinities, an innumerable mortal number will arise. Hence anyone who wishes to have more methods of writing by metathesis, and ones removed from our instruction, if he is even a little ingenious and diligent, will obtain an easy result in his work. For the human intellect can do very great things if it is aided by study and art. But he who despises the smallest things will never attain to greater ones. I know that there will be very many who will deride these studies of ours as empty and childish; to them we give as a reply that we shall be wholly content, provided they please those at whose insistence they have been composed by us.

The straight table follows.

The Straight Table of Transposition.

[A transposition grid of the 24-letter alphabet (a b d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t u x y z w), each successive row shifted by one — rendered as printed.]

In this canonical or straight table of letters you have, from our one and usual [alphabet] of Latin letters themselves, by their permutation or transposition, as many alphabets as there are monograms throughout it—namely four-and-twenty times twenty-four, which make in number 576; and multiplied by as many again, they yield a little less than fourteen thousand.

[d ij]

The Reverse Table of Transposition.

[A reverse transposition grid, as printed.]

In this reverse table you have, by the transposition of letters, as many alphabets as we likewise marked out in the preceding straight [table]. For, as you see, under the metathesis there are 24 to the right; to the left likewise as many; downward 24. Which, multiplied 24 times by 98, reduced in the form of a cross to the four sides, make alphabets not fewer than 112.

There follows the same table expanded.

IOANNES TRITHEIVS ABBAS PEAPOLITANVS Lectori S. CVm literae Graecorum et amp; Hebraeorum omnes sint numerales, sepe miratus sum quod curiosa priscorũ latinitas etiã suas literas nume- rorum ratione subseruire non fecit. Hebraei quarundam duplicita te litterarũ notas octo et amp; uiginti ad omnem numerum sufficientes institue runt. Graeci uero hunc literarum defectum quatuor appositione characte rum simili prouidentia subleuarunt Nos ergo cum 200 literas quatuor ha- bentes et amp; uiginti, quare et amp; nostras non facimus numerales, qui similiter quatuor possumus inuenire duplicatas? Demus quatuor in exemplum, etsa tis omnem erit ad numerum, m et amp; ij finale. item s lon- gum et amp; s finale siue clausum . itẽ v clausum et amp; u apertum. His dum xxiij. literas usuales adiungimus, octo et amp; uigini numeris sufficiens omnibus characteres habemus. Eritque haud magni laboris negocium hunc numera- di apprehendere modum, his qui litteras iam nouerunt, si eum semel me- moriae commendauerint. Poterit enim haec noctra inventio multis esse pro ficua, quoniam paucis literis multa milia compraehendit in numero, quae omnia primo intuitu sine calculatione aliqua luce clarius discerni possunt et amp; intelligi. Quod fieri per figuras algariti praesertim in numeris mag nis tam facilè non posse multis uidetur, minus in arte calculatoria exper tis. Mox enim ut oculo numerum quantumlibet magnum inspexeri eum et amp; plene intelligere, &amp; exprimere poteris sine circumlocutione seu diui sione sermonis. Quod quam fit facile conueniens est ut litteras ipsas in numerum redactas consignemus. Scripsi XVI. Martij Anno M.D.VIII. |a|b|c|d|e|f|g|h|i|k|l|m|n|o|p|r|q;s;t;u;x;y;z; |A|B|C|D|E|F|G|H|I|K|L|M|N|O|P|R|Q;S;T;U;X;Y;Z;

In the present orchema a multiple alphabet is handed down through transposition and leap, both by the rule of order and by the position of the letters. All these things suffice as an example for those who cannot be content with the things set in place, so that they may have a method and form for discovering the things that remain, because they can be varied without number.

nte omnem inuentionem et usum literarum in primordio mundi cum homines adhuc rudes essent ingenio et moribus inculti, sub tribum communicatione uicissitudinis regimen, ut quidam opinan tur intelligentiarum per annos mille sexaginta tres sibi per ordinem suc cedentes, erant in orbe planetarum influentia corporibus in terra suo mo do praestantes. Dicunt huius rei speculatores antiqui Saturnum à mundi principio germinatis in terra nascentibus praefuisse influendo principali ter sua moderante intelligentia, quam Orisielem, hoc est uiificantem dei nuncuparunt, annis lunaribus trecentis quinquaginta quatuor, mensibus item quatuor, ac diebus horisque totidē. Quae nos ut poetica recensemus, nō confirmamus. Post Saturnũ Venus, post Venerẽ Iupiter dominii ponitur assumpfisse. Post Iouem uero Mercurius in ordine quartus dominator, in gemia hominum diueris artibus decorauit. Sub tribus autem intelligentijs memoratis Saturno uidelicet, Venere, et Ioue dominantibus, afferunt ho mimes non babuisse usum uel notitiam literarum. Vnde quotiens alter alte ri uoluisset aliquid nunciare secreti, non id scriptis cum officium defue rit literarum, sed quibusdam similitudinibus animalium, arborum et plan tarum, seu aliorum sensibilium alicius prout inter se quique conuenerant symbolicè faciebant. Saturni tempus mores dedit, ut aiunt, hominibus in fluentie propriè conuenientes. Fecit enim agricultores, uenatores, conde tores urbiũm, rudes, siluae tres, tristes, simplices, uita et moribus incultos, f ii &amp; longo tempore in carne uiuentes·Post orifielẽ Saturni sicut ipsi taliter opinantes, dicunt intelligentiam regimen orbis influendo·Anael motor Veneris accipiens trecentis quinquaginta quatuor annis, mensibus, die¬bisq́; &amp; horis quatuor continuauit, sub quo homines coeperunt esse cul¬tiores, domos construere crebrius et urbes, uarias quoq́; artes inuenire ma nuales, opus uidelicet textrinũ, lanificium, et his alia similia plura·Carnis ctiam uoluptatibus per amplius defluere coeperunt, uxoresq́; desumere pul chras, &amp; procreatis filijs ex eis multis, à naturali simplicitate notabiliter defluxerũt·Ludos, cãtilenas inuenerũt, cithara canere coeperunt, et quic quid ad Veneris confirmant pertinere influentiã, motũ carnis nimium sequentes studiosius excogitabāt·Tertiam Iouis intelligentiam nominabant Zacharielẽ, quae dominiũ suscipiens mundi post Anaelẽ fecit homines do minandi cupiditate inquietos, uenationes agere, tentoria facere, &amp; se ua rijs indumentis exornare·Facta est eo dominante pro Iouis qualitate, qui patrem regno priuauit, magna inter bonos et amp; malos diuisio, illis Deum in uocantibus, istis uero carni deditis et amp; mundo·Sub eo regimine Adam primus homo est mortuus, testamentum omni relinquens posteritati semel mo riendi·Quartus uero motor seu angelus Mercurij Raphael post Zacharielem influens mundanis, coepit anno millesimo quinquagesimo quinto in fine mensis Februarij, &amp; durauit usque ad annum mun¬di millesimum quadringentesimum decimum, sub quo literarum usus primo dicitur inuentus·Fuerunt autem aliae litterae tunc, ut referunt, ab his quas mundus hodie habet multum diuersae, ad formam et amp; similitudinem ar borum, plantarum et amp; animalium excogitatae, quae tamen cum tempore po stea multipliciter sunt immutatae, facilioremq́; formandi modũ sumpserũt et ornatum cultiorem·Mercurium enim figmenta poetarum omnis literaturae praesidem esse dixerunt, magna latere sabulis rerum arcana promittentes·Humano posthaec multiplicato genere, &amp; in omnem terram ubiq́; diffuso, non diu mansit unitas literarum, sed corporum et amp; animorum procul ab inuicem diuisio, diuerfos et amp; uarios inuenit modos scribendi, de quibus longa nobis naratio·Plato Philosophus in Phoedro, literas usumq́; scribendi.

Johannes Trithemius, [unclear] abbot, greets the reader.

Since the letters of the Greeks and the Hebrews are all numerical, I have often wondered that the careful Latin usage of the ancients did not also make its own letters serve in the reckoning of numbers. The Hebrews, by duplicating certain letters, established twenty-eight signs, sufficient for every number. The Greeks, with like foresight, remedied this deficiency of letters by adding four characters. Since we therefore have twenty-four letters, why do we not make ours numerical too, we who can similarly find four duplicated letters? Let us give four as an example, and there will be enough for every number: [unclear] and final [j?]; likewise long s and final or closed s; likewise closed v and open u. When we add these to the twenty-three usual letters, we have twenty-eight characters sufficient for all numbers. And it will be no great labor to grasp this method of numbering for those who already know the letters, if they once commit it to memory. For this invention of ours will be able to be useful to many, since in a few letters it comprises many thousands in number, all of which can be discerned and understood at first sight, more clearly than light, without any calculation. Many who are less experienced in the art of calculation think that this cannot be done so easily by the figures of algorism, especially in large numbers. For as soon as you have looked with your eye upon a number, however large, you will be able both to understand it fully and to express it without circumlocution or division of speech. Since this is so easy, it is fitting that we set down the letters themselves reduced to number. I wrote this on 16 March in the year 1508.

Behold, reader, you have the method by which you can adequately set down and write every writable number in a few letters, whose extension, as you see, proceeds to infinity. But as it was once customary to say in a proverb, the tired ox plants his foot firmly: whoever wishes to be content with the former things should follow the old method of numbering. So that those who do not know it may understand it more easily, it will not be tedious for me to give in what follows the form which Hunibald, historiographer of the Franks, and also Bede, Rabanus, Helperic, monks, and several of the ancients used in chronicles and ecclesiastical calculations, as follows.

We have set forth up to this point, by way of example, the ancient manner of the Germans and Franks of writing numbers with Latin letters, so that we might also furnish knowledge of it to those who do not know it. But as for the fact that, in the placement of the figures of algorism, we have departed from the common rule of computation, this was done not from error but for a reasonable cause, namely so that we should not be overburdened in an excessive progression. There were also some who wrote larger numbers in this manner.

Huius alphabeti ministerio Nortmanni quicquid inter se uoluissebant. Quam scribendi rationem graecorum nemo intelligere potuit, quoniam et si omnes characteres isti sint Graecoquia tamen literas ex ordine numerali repraesentant latinas, neque à Graeco legi poterunt, neque à Latino, qui huius industriae scientiam non prius fuerit assecutus. Poterit etiam hic modus scribendi multipliciter variari, quando per methatensis numeri mutantur et litterae. Quod et in litris graecis fieri potest solidis ad uotum et arbitrium industriosi cuiusque scri bentis. Nec erit modus formandi characteres istos multum difficilis, illima xime qui fuerit aliquantulum usitus. Satis etiam praescripti characteres linguae conueniunt germanice, cum quibus omnia nobis possimus denota re occurrentia, in qualibet fuerimus locutione periti. Quotiens iota per se ponitur, ut sciatur de notare literam ℓ. decimam alphabeti sic ī, supe rius motatur. DE ALPHABETO ET ratione scribendi veterum Francorum. [unclear] G Ermãs olim literas habuisse à Graecis plurimorium opinio tenet, quos et sermone usos Graeco maximè insacris suis constanter affir mant. Dicunt enim magnam inter Graecam linguaem nostram extinxit penitus. Doctissimus ille quondam preceptor meus Ioannes Camerarius Dalburgius, Ecclesiae Vuormaciensis reuerendissimus an tistes aliquot milia dictionum Graecarum collegerat, quae in utraque lingua Graeca et Germanica idem significant. Et Drudas priscos in Gallia Pontifices sacrorum Graeco sermone usos fuisse maxime in sacris, Caesar testa tur in commentarijs. Verum Romanis orbem devastantibus, suarum usu literarum tandem cum dominio multis nationibus uiolenter imposuerunt. Before all invention and use of letters, in the beginning of the world, when human beings were still crude in understanding and uncultivated in manners, under the [unclear] governance of alternation, as some suppose, of the intelligences, succeeding one another in order for one thousand sixty-three years, they were, in the sphere of the planets, by their influence exercising power in their own fashion over bodies on earth. The ancient speculators on this matter say that Saturn, from the beginning of the world, presided by his influence over things germinating and springing up on the earth, principally through his governing intelligence, which they called Orisiel, that is, “the vivifier of God,” for three hundred fifty-four lunar years, likewise four months, and the same number of days and hours. We recount these things as poetic fictions; we do not affirm them. After Saturn, Venus; after Venus, Jupiter is said to have assumed dominion. But after Jupiter, Mercury, fourth ruler in order, adorned the talents of human beings with various arts. Under the three intelligences just mentioned, namely while Saturn, Venus, and Jupiter were ruling, they report that human beings did not have the use or knowledge of letters. Hence whenever one person wished to announce some secret matter to another, he did this not by writings, since the service of letters was lacking, but symbolically, by certain likenesses of animals, trees and plants, or of some other perceptible things, according as each had agreed among themselves. The time of Saturn, they say, gave to human beings manners properly corresponding to his influence. For it made them farmers, hunters, founders of cities, crude, woodland-dwelling, gloomy, simple, uncultivated in life and manners, and living for a long time in the flesh. After Orisiel of Saturn, as those who hold such opinions say, the intelligence Anael, mover of Venus, receiving the governance of the world by influence, continued it for three hundred fifty-four years, months, days, and four hours. Under him human beings began to be more cultivated, to construct houses more frequently and cities, and also to invent various manual arts, namely the work of weaving, wool-working, and many other things similar to these. They also began to flow more fully into the pleasures of the flesh, and to take beautiful wives; and with many children begotten from them, they notably fell away from natural simplicity. They invented games and songs, began to play the cithara, and whatever they affirm to pertain to the influence of Venus they devised more zealously, following the impulse of the flesh too much. They named the third intelligence, that of Jupiter, Zachariel; and when it took up dominion of the world after Anael, it made human beings restless with desire to rule, to go hunting, to make tents, and to adorn themselves with various garments. While he ruled, in accordance with the quality of Jupiter, who deprived his father of the kingdom, there arose a great division between the good and the bad, the former calling upon God, the latter devoted to the flesh and the world. Under that governance Adam, the first man, died, leaving to all posterity the testament of dying once. But the fourth mover or angel of Mercury, Raphael, influencing worldly things after Zachariel, began in the one thousand fifty-fifth year, at the end of the month of February, and lasted until the one thousand four hundred tenth year of the world. Under him the use of letters is first said to have been invented. The letters then were, as they report, very different from those which the world has today, devised according to the form and likeness of trees, plants, and animals; yet these afterwards, over time, were altered in many ways, and assumed an easier manner of being formed and a more cultivated ornament. For the fictions of the poets said that Mercury was the presiding power over all literature, promising that great hidden secrets of things lay concealed in fables. After this, when the human race had multiplied and been spread everywhere over the whole earth, the unity of letters did not long remain; but the separation of bodies and minds far from one another discovered diverse and varied modes of writing, about which a long narration would be required from us. Plato the Philosopher, in the Phaedrus, letters and the use of writing.

[he] relates that a certain philosopher, Theut by name, first discovered the art of writing, and at the same time the reckoning of weights and numbers and a certain game of dice, and taught Thamus, king of the Egyptians. But concerning the other ancient men who are said to have handed down special letters to almost individual nations and peoples, which remain in use among them down to the present day, it is not my purpose on this occasion to set down or describe the account. For all the more learned men among us know that Cadmus, son of Agenor, king of the Phoenicians, is said first to have brought sixteen letters into Greece: α. β. γ. δ. ε. ζ. ι. λ. μ. ν. ο. π. ϱ. σ. τ. ψ. To these Palamedes, at the time of the Trojan War, is said to have added four: ξ. θ. φ. χ. And Pythagoras afterwards added the letter θ, so that there should be twenty-one. χ. κ. ω. were subsequently discovered by others. Gordanis, bishop of the Goths, gave his people letters proper to them. When the unity of language had been confounded, the simplicity of characters too was variously altered in many ways. Hence it came about that, in the course of time, the use of letters arrogated to itself such licence that not only individual peoples, but also particular men, fashioning new characters for letters at their own discretion, prepared hiding-places for their mysteries. Yet every writing in an unusual character will not be free from the suspicion of those who see it. Notwithstanding this, many kings, tyrants, and princes of old devised for themselves a manner of writing set apart from common use and familiar to themselves, taking thought for the suspicion of others, provided only that what they wished to remain secret was not perceived. In imitation of these, I, [unclear], wishing to bring this work of Polygraphy, as far as possible, to a completed end, have resolved in this sixth book, which is the last, to call back from the underworld certain characters of the ancients which have now passed out of human use, lest they perish utterly. First, then, we shall set down the ancient manner of writing of the Northmen.

Concerning the alphabet and the remarkable manner of writing of the Northmen, at the time when they were laying waste Gaul by their incursion.

All the letters of the Greeks and Palestinians are numerical, as was said before, while of the Latins, which we Germans also use, only seven are referred to numbers, namely c, d, i, l, m, v, and x. But the Northmen, after they had once come forth with the Asiatic Dacians from the Scandian islands, which are now called Gothic, wandered through Gaul for more than forty years and devastated it most grievously. In order to take counsel for their secret affairs, as Bede the English monk testifies, they discovered from the letters of the Greeks a new and beautiful manner of writing, as follows. For they adapted the numbers of the Greeks, comprised in ten letters among the twenty-four letters, to Latin characters, and prudently hid our letters beneath a foreign form: that is, in the manner in which we use numbers in place of letters, when, for example, for a we put 1, for b 2, for c 3, for d 4, and so on consecutively to the end of the alphabet. It is indeed a beautiful and quite safe invention, which neither a Greek nor a Latin will easily understand. For the whole alphabet is not found in it, but only nine letters, and one numerical sign, namely g, which among them signifies six and in this manner of writing denotes f, the sixth letter of the Latins. Moreover, yielding to our German language, in which we were born, we have finally added w, double v, as the twenty-fourth letter of our nation, which, according to the Greek number, we have formed thus: kΛ. But we shall set down this writing of the Northmen from the following order of Greek letters, in imitation of them.
